title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Colonies.
Part I. The Motives for Establishing New Colonies.
The motive behind the first European settlements in America and the West Indies was not as plain and obvious as the one that drove the colonies of ancient Greece and Rome.

Each of the various states of ancient Greece held only a very small territory. Whenever the population of any one of them grew beyond what its land could comfortably support, some of the people were sent off to find a new home in some remote, distant part of the world, since the warlike neighbours pressing in on every side made it hard for any state to expand its territory much at home. The Dorian colonies went mainly to Italy and Sicily, which in the period before Rome was founded were inhabited by barbarous and uncivilized peoples. The colonies of the Ionians and Aeolians, the two other great Greek tribes, went to Asia Minor and the islands of the Aegean Sea, whose inhabitants at that time seem to have been in much the same condition as those of Sicily and Italy. The mother city always regarded the colony as a child entitled to great favour and assistance, and owing much gratitude and respect in return; but it treated it as an emancipated child over whom it claimed no direct authority or jurisdiction. The colony set up its own form of government, passed its own laws, elected its own magistrates, and made peace or war with its neighbours as an independent state, with no need to wait for the mother city's approval or consent. Nothing could be plainer or more obvious than the motive behind each of these foundings.

Rome, like most of the other ancient republics, was originally founded on an agrarian law that divided the public territory in fixed proportions among the various citizens who made up the state. The ordinary course of events, through marriage, inheritance, and sale, inevitably disturbed this original division, and often the lands set aside to support many different families ended up in the hands of a single person. To cure this disorder, as it was thought to be, a law was passed limiting the amount of land any citizen could own to five hundred jugera, about 350 English acres. Yet this law, though we read of its being enforced on one or two occasions, was either ignored or evaded, and the inequality of fortunes kept growing. Most citizens owned no land, and without land the customs of those times made it hard for a free man to keep his independence. Today, even if a poor man owns no land, he can either farm someone else's land if he has a little capital, or run some small retail trade; and if he has no capital at all, he can find work as a farm labourer or a craftsman. But among the ancient Romans the lands of the rich were all worked by slaves, supervised by an overseer who was himself a slave, so a poor free man had little chance of being hired as a farmer or a labourer. All trades and crafts too, even retail trade, were carried on by the slaves of the rich for their masters' profit, and those masters' wealth, authority, and protection made it hard for a poor free man to compete with them. So citizens with no land had scarcely any way to survive except the handouts of candidates at the annual elections. Whenever the tribunes wanted to stir the people up against the rich and powerful, they reminded them of the old land divisions and presented the law that limited this kind of private property as the fundamental law of the republic. The people clamoured for land, and the rich and powerful, we can be sure, were entirely resolved to give them none of theirs. To satisfy them to some degree, then, they often proposed sending out a new colony. But conquering Rome, even on such occasions, had no need to turn its citizens loose to seek their fortunes across the wide world without knowing where they would settle. It generally assigned them lands in the conquered provinces of Italy, where, being within the republic's dominions, they could never form an independent state, but were at best a kind of corporation that, though it had the power to pass its own bye-laws, was always subject to the correction, jurisdiction, and legislative authority of the mother city. Sending out a colony of this sort not only gave the people some satisfaction, but often established a kind of garrison in a newly conquered province whose loyalty might otherwise have been doubtful. So a Roman colony, whether we look at the nature of the settlement itself or the motives for creating it, was entirely different from a Greek one. The words used in the original languages for these different settlements have very different meanings to match. The Latin word colonia simply means a plantation. The Greek word apoikia, by contrast, means a separation of dwelling, a departure from home, a going out of the house. But although Roman colonies differed in many ways from Greek ones, the motive that prompted both was equally plain and obvious. Both kinds of institution arose either from irresistible necessity or from clear and obvious advantage.

The European colonies in America and the West Indies arose from no necessity, and although they have produced very great benefits, those benefits are not nearly so clear and obvious. They were not understood when the colonies were first established, and were not the motive either for that establishment or for the discoveries that led to it; and the nature, extent, and limits of that benefit are perhaps still not well understood today.

During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries the Venetians ran a very profitable trade in spices and other East Indian goods, which they distributed among the other nations of Europe. They bought these goods mainly in Egypt, then ruled by the Mamelukes, who were enemies of the Turks, and the Venetians were also enemies of the Turks. This shared interest, backed by Venetian money, created a connection that gave Venice almost a monopoly on the trade.

The great profits of the Venetians stirred the greed of the Portuguese. Throughout the fifteenth century they had been trying to find a sea route to the countries from which the Moors brought them ivory and gold dust across the desert. They discovered the Madeiras, the Canaries, the Azores, the Cape Verde islands, the coast of Guinea, and those of Loango, Congo, Angola, and Benguela, and finally the Cape of Good Hope. They had long wanted a share in the Venetians' profitable trade, and this last discovery opened up a real prospect of getting it. In 1497 Vasco da Gama sailed from Lisbon with a fleet of four ships, and after eleven months at sea reached the coast of Hindustan, completing a course of discoveries that had been pursued steadily, with very little interruption, for nearly a century.

Some years before this, while Europe was still in suspense about the Portuguese projects, whose success still looked uncertain, a Genoese navigator formed the even bolder plan of sailing to the East Indies by going west. The location of those countries was at that time very poorly known in Europe. The few European travellers who had been there had exaggerated the distance, perhaps out of simple ignorance, since what was genuinely vast seemed almost infinite to people who had no way to measure it, or perhaps to make their own adventures in visiting such remote regions seem even more marvellous. The longer the eastward route was, Columbus rightly concluded, the shorter the westward route would be. He therefore proposed to take the western route, as both the shortest and the surest, and he had the good luck to convince Isabella of Castile that his plan was likely to work. He sailed from the port of Palos in August 1492, nearly five years before Vasco da Gama set out from Portugal, and after a voyage of two to three months he discovered first some of the small Bahama or Lucayan islands, and then the great island of Saint Domingo.

But the countries Columbus discovered, on this voyage or any later one, bore no resemblance to the ones he had set out to find. Instead of the wealth, cultivation, and dense population of China and Hindustan, all he found in Saint Domingo and every other part of the new world he ever visited was a land entirely covered with forest, uncultivated, and inhabited only by some tribes of naked and miserable savages. Even so, he was reluctant to believe these were not some of the countries described by Marco Polo, the first European to visit China or the East Indies, or at least the first to leave any description of them; and a very slight resemblance, such as the one he found between Cibao, a mountain in Saint Domingo, and Cipango, mentioned by Marco Polo, was often enough to send him back to this favourite idea, even against the clearest evidence. In his letters to Ferdinand and Isabella he called the countries he had discovered the Indies. He had no doubt that they were the far edge of the lands Marco Polo had described, and that they lay not far from the Ganges or from the countries Alexander had conquered. Even when he was finally convinced they were different, he still flattered himself that those rich countries were close by, and on a later voyage he accordingly went looking for them along the coast of Terra Firma and towards the Isthmus of Darien.

Because of this mistake by Columbus, the name of the Indies has clung to those unlucky countries ever since; and when it was finally established that the new Indies were entirely different from the old, the former were called the West Indies, in contrast to the latter, which were called the East Indies.

It mattered to Columbus, however, that the countries he had discovered, whatever they were, should be presented to the Spanish court as of very great importance; and in what makes up the real wealth of any country, the animal and vegetable products of the soil, there was at that time nothing that could really justify such a portrayal of them.

The cori, something between a rat and a rabbit, and thought by Mr Buffon to be the same as the aperea of Brazil, was the largest live-bearing quadruped in Saint Domingo. The species seems never to have been very numerous, and the dogs and cats of the Spaniards are said to have almost entirely wiped it out long ago, along with some other still smaller kinds. These animals, however, together with a fairly large lizard called the ivana or iguana, made up the main part of the animal food the land provided.

The inhabitants' plant food, though not very plentiful because of their lack of industry, was not quite so scanty. It consisted of Indian corn, yams, potatoes, bananas, and the like, plants then completely unknown in Europe and never since much valued there, or thought to provide nourishment equal to what comes from the ordinary grains and pulses that have been cultivated in this part of the world since time out of mind.

The cotton plant, however, supplied the raw material of a very important manufacture, and was at that time, to Europeans, undoubtedly the most valuable of all the plant products of those islands. But although by the end of the fifteenth century the muslins and other cotton goods of the East Indies were much prized throughout Europe, the cotton manufacture itself was not practised anywhere in Europe. So even this product could not at that time strike Europeans as being of much importance.

Finding nothing among the animals or plants of the newly discovered countries to justify a glowing account of them, Columbus turned his attention to their minerals, flattering himself that the richness of this third kingdom would fully make up for the insignificance of the other two. The little bits of gold the inhabitants used to decorate their clothes, which he was told they often found in the streams and torrents running down from the mountains, were enough to convince him that those mountains held the richest gold mines. Saint Domingo was therefore presented as a country rich in gold, and on that account, given the prejudices not only of our own day but of those times, an inexhaustible source of real wealth for the crown and kingdom of Spain. When Columbus returned from his first voyage and was received with a kind of triumphal honour by the sovereigns of Castile and Aragon, the chief products of the countries he had discovered were carried in solemn procession before him. The only valuable part of them was some small bands, bracelets, and other gold ornaments, along with some bales of cotton. The rest were mere objects of common wonder and curiosity: some reeds of extraordinary size, some birds with very beautiful plumage, and some stuffed skins of the huge alligator and manatee. Leading the procession were six or seven of the wretched natives, whose strange colour and appearance added greatly to the novelty of the spectacle.

On the strength of Columbus's reports, the council of Castile resolved to take possession of countries whose inhabitants were plainly incapable of defending themselves. The pious goal of converting them to Christianity gave the injustice of the project a veneer of holiness. But the hope of finding treasures of gold there was the only real motive for undertaking it; and to give this motive more weight, Columbus proposed that half of all the gold and silver found there should belong to the crown. The council approved this proposal.

As long as all, or most, of the gold the first adventurers brought back to Europe was got by the very easy method of plundering the defenceless natives, paying even this heavy tax was perhaps not very hard. But once the natives had been completely stripped of everything they had, which in Saint Domingo and all the other countries Columbus discovered was done within six or eight years, and once it became necessary to dig the gold out of mines to find more, paying the tax was no longer possible. The rigorous collection of it, they say, first caused the total abandonment of the mines of Saint Domingo, which have never been worked since. The tax was therefore soon cut to a third, then a fifth, then a tenth, and finally a twentieth of the gross output of the gold mines. The tax on silver remained a fifth of the gross output for a long time. It was only cut to a tenth during the present century. But the first adventurers do not seem to have cared much about silver. Nothing less precious than gold seemed worth their attention.

All the other Spanish ventures in the New World after Columbus's seem to have been driven by the same motive. It was the sacred thirst for gold that carried Oviedo, Nicuesa, and Vasco Núñez de Balboa to the Isthmus of Darien; that carried Cortés to Mexico, and Almagro and Pizarro to Chile and Peru. Whenever these adventurers reached an unknown coast, their first question was always whether there was any gold to be found there; and according to what they learned about this, they decided either to leave the country or to settle in it.

Of all these costly and uncertain ventures, which bankrupt most of the people who take them on, none is perhaps more thoroughly ruinous than the search for new gold and silver mines. It is perhaps the most disadvantageous lottery in the world, the one in which the winnings of those who draw the prizes bear the smallest proportion to the losses of those who draw the blanks; for although the prizes are few and the blanks many, the usual price of a ticket is the entire fortune of a very rich man. Mining ventures, instead of restoring the capital put into them along with the ordinary profit on that capital, usually swallow up both capital and profit. They are therefore the ventures to which a prudent lawgiver who wanted to increase his nation's capital would least want to give any special encouragement, or to draw a larger share of that capital than would flow to them of its own accord. In fact, almost all people have such absurd confidence in their own good luck that wherever there is the slightest chance of success, too large a share of capital tends to go that way on its own.

But although the judgment of sober reason and experience about such ventures has always been extremely unfavourable, human greed has commonly judged quite otherwise. The same passion that has prompted so many people with the absurd idea of the philosopher's stone has prompted others with the equally absurd idea of immensely rich gold and silver mines. They failed to consider that the value of those metals has in all ages and nations come chiefly from their scarcity, that their scarcity comes from the very small quantities nature has deposited anywhere in one place, from the hard and stubborn materials with which she has almost everywhere surrounded those small quantities, and therefore from the labour and expense everywhere needed to break through to them and get at them. They imagined that veins of those metals might be found in many places, as large and abundant as the veins commonly found of lead, copper, tin, or iron. Sir Walter Raleigh's dream of the golden city and country of El Dorado may show us that even wise men are not always free of such strange delusions. More than a hundred years after that great man's death, the Jesuit Gumilla was still convinced that wonderful country was real, and expressed with great warmth, and I dare say great sincerity, how glad he would be to carry the light of the gospel to a people who could so well reward the pious labours of their missionary.

In the countries first discovered by the Spaniards, there are at present no known gold or silver mines thought worth working. The quantities of those metals the first adventurers are said to have found there had probably been greatly exaggerated, as had the richness of the mines worked immediately after the first discovery. Yet what those adventurers were reported to have found was enough to inflame the greed of all their countrymen. Every Spaniard who sailed to America expected to find an El Dorado. And here fortune did what she has done on very few other occasions: she partly realized the extravagant hopes of her devotees. In the discovery and conquest of Mexico and Peru, which happened about thirty and about forty years respectively after Columbus's first expedition, she presented them with something not very unlike the profusion of precious metals they had been seeking.

So a commercial venture aimed at the East Indies led to the first discovery of the West. A venture of conquest led to all the Spanish settlements in those newly discovered countries. The motive that drove them to conquest was a project of gold and silver mines; and a chain of accidents that no human foresight could have predicted made this project far more successful than the adventurers had any reasonable grounds to expect.

The first adventurers from all the other European nations who tried to make settlements in America were driven by the same fanciful hopes, but they were not equally successful. It was more than a hundred years after the first settlement of Brazil before any silver, gold, or diamond mines were discovered there. In the English, French, Dutch, and Danish colonies none have ever been discovered, at least none currently thought worth working. The first English settlers in North America, however, offered the king a fifth of all the gold and silver that should be found there as an inducement to grant them their patents. In the patents of Sir Walter Raleigh, of the London and Plymouth companies, of the council of Plymouth, and others, this fifth was duly reserved to the crown. To the hope of finding gold and silver mines those first settlers also added the hope of discovering a north-west passage to the East Indies. So far they have been disappointed in both.
Part II. Causes of the Prosperity of New Colonies.

The colony of a civilized nation that takes over either an empty country or one so thinly populated that the natives readily make way for the new settlers advances toward wealth and greatness faster than any other human society.

The colonists bring with them a knowledge of agriculture and other useful arts far beyond what could develop on its own over many centuries among savage and barbarous nations. They also bring the habit of obedience, some notion of the orderly government found in their own country, of the system of laws that supports it, and of a regular administration of justice; and they naturally set up something similar in the new settlement. But among savage and barbarous nations the natural progress of law and government is even slower than the natural progress of the arts, once law and government have been established far enough to protect those arts. Every colonist gets more land than he can possibly cultivate. He has no rent and scarcely any taxes to pay. No landlord takes a share of his produce, and the sovereign's share is usually just a trifle. So he has every reason to make as large as possible a produce that will be almost entirely his own. But his land is usually so vast that, with all his own effort and all the effort of any others he can hire, he can rarely make it yield a tenth of what it is capable of producing. He is therefore eager to gather labourers from everywhere and reward them with the most generous wages. But those generous wages, combined with the abundance and cheapness of land, soon make those labourers leave him to become landlords themselves, and to reward other labourers just as generously, who soon leave them for the same reason they left their first master. The generous reward of labour encourages marriage. The children, in their tender years of infancy, are well fed and properly cared for; and when they grow up, the value of their labour more than repays the cost of their upbringing. When they reach adulthood, the high price of labour and the low price of land let them set themselves up just as their fathers did before them.

In other countries, rent and profit eat up wages, and the two upper classes oppress the lower one; but in new colonies the interest of the two upper classes forces them to treat the lower one with more generosity and humanity, at least where that lower class is not enslaved. Empty lands of the greatest natural fertility can be had for next to nothing. The increase in revenue the owner, who is always the entrepreneur, expects from improving them makes up his profit, which in these circumstances is usually very great; but this great profit cannot be made without employing other people's labour to clear and cultivate the land, and the mismatch between the vast extent of the land and the small number of people, which is usual in new colonies, makes it hard for him to get that labour. So he does not haggle over wages, but is willing to hire labour at any price. The high wages of labour encourage population growth. The cheapness and abundance of good land encourage improvement and allow the owner to pay those high wages. Almost the entire price of the land consists in those wages; and although they are high considered as wages, they are low considered as the price of something so valuable. Whatever encourages the growth of population and improvement encourages the growth of real wealth and greatness.

The progress of many of the ancient Greek colonies toward wealth and greatness seems accordingly to have been very rapid. Within a century or two, several of them appear to have rivalled, and even surpassed, their mother cities. Syracuse and Agrigentum in Sicily, Tarentum and Locri in Italy, and Ephesus and Miletus in Asia Minor appear by all accounts to have been at least equal to any of the cities of ancient Greece. Though established later, all the refined arts, philosophy, poetry, and eloquence, seem to have been cultivated as early and developed as highly in them as anywhere in the mother country. The schools of the two oldest Greek philosophers, Thales and Pythagoras, were founded, remarkably, not in ancient Greece, but one in an Asiatic and the other in an Italian colony. All these colonies had settled in countries inhabited by savage and barbarous nations who readily made way for the new settlers. They had plenty of good land, and since they were wholly independent of the mother city, they were free to manage their own affairs in whatever way they judged best for their own interest.

The history of the Roman colonies is nowhere near as brilliant. Some of them, such as Florence, did over the course of many ages, and after the fall of the mother city, grow into considerable states. But none of them seems ever to have advanced very rapidly. They were all founded in conquered provinces, which in most cases had already been fully populated. The amount of land assigned to each colonist was seldom very large, and since the colony was not independent, they were not always free to manage their own affairs in whatever way they judged best for their own interest.

In the abundance of good land, the European colonies in America and the West Indies resemble, and even greatly surpass, those of ancient Greece. In their dependence on the mother state they resemble those of ancient Rome; but their great distance from Europe has in all of them softened the effects of this dependence to some degree. Their situation has put them less in the view, and less in the power, of their mother country. In pursuing their own interest their own way, their conduct has on many occasions been overlooked, either because it was not known or not understood in Europe, and on some occasions it has simply been tolerated and accepted, because the distance made it hard to restrain. Even the violent and arbitrary government of Spain has often been forced to recall or soften the orders it had issued for governing its colonies, for fear of a general uprising. The progress of all the European colonies in wealth, population, and improvement has accordingly been very great.

From the moment its colonies were first established, the crown of Spain drew some revenue from them through its share of the gold and silver. It was also a revenue of a kind to excite in human greed the most extravagant expectation of still greater riches. So the Spanish colonies, from the moment they were first established, drew a great deal of attention from their mother country, while those of the other European nations were for a long time largely neglected. The former perhaps did not thrive any better because of this attention, nor the latter any worse because of this neglect. In proportion to the extent of the country they to some degree occupy, the Spanish colonies are reckoned less populous and thriving than those of almost any other European nation. Even so, the Spanish colonies' progress in population and improvement has certainly been very rapid and very great. The city of Lima, founded since the conquest, is described by Ulloa as containing fifty thousand inhabitants nearly thirty years ago. Quito, which had been only a miserable hamlet of Indians, is described by the same author as being equally populous in his own time. Gemelli Careri, a supposed traveller it is said, but who seems everywhere to have written from very good information, describes the city of Mexico as containing a hundred thousand inhabitants, a number which, despite all the exaggerations of the Spanish writers, is probably more than five times what it held in the time of Montezuma. These figures greatly exceed those of Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, the three largest cities of the English colonies. Before the Spanish conquest there were no draught animals fit for hauling in either Mexico or Peru. The lama was their only beast of burden, and its strength seems to have been a good deal less than that of a common ass. The plough was unknown to them. They had no knowledge of iron. They had no coined money, nor any established medium of trade of any kind. Their commerce was carried on by barter. A kind of wooden spade was their main farming tool. Sharp stones served them as knives and hatchets to cut with; fish bones and the hard sinews of certain animals served them as needles to sew with; and these seem to have been their main tools of trade. In such a state of things, it seems impossible that either of these empires could have been as improved or as well cultivated as it is now, when they are plentifully supplied with all kinds of European livestock, and when the use of iron, the plough, and many of the arts of Europe have been introduced among them. But the populousness of any country must be in proportion to the degree of its improvement and cultivation. Despite the cruel destruction of the natives that followed the conquest, these two great empires are probably more populous now than they ever were before; and the people are surely very different, for we must admit, I think, that the Spanish creoles are in many respects superior to the ancient Indians.

After the Spanish settlements, that of the Portuguese in Brazil is the oldest of any European nation in America. But because for a long time after its first discovery no gold or silver mines were found there, and it therefore yielded little or no revenue to the crown, it was for a long time largely neglected; and during this neglect it grew into a great and powerful colony. While Portugal was under Spanish rule, Brazil was attacked by the Dutch, who seized seven of the fourteen provinces into which it is divided. They expected soon to conquer the other seven, when Portugal regained its independence by raising the family of Braganza to the throne. The Dutch, as enemies of the Spaniards, then became friends of the Portuguese, who were likewise enemies of the Spaniards. So they agreed to leave the part of Brazil they had not conquered to the king of Portugal, who agreed to leave the part they had conquered to them, as not worth quarrelling over with such good allies. But the Dutch government soon began to oppress the Portuguese colonists, who, instead of wasting their time on complaints, took up arms against their new masters, and by their own courage and resolve, with the connivance, though without any open assistance, of the mother country, drove them out of Brazil. The Dutch, finding it impossible to hold any part of the country for themselves, were therefore content to have it restored entirely to the crown of Portugal. This colony is said to hold more than six hundred thousand people, either Portuguese or of Portuguese descent, creoles, mulattoes, and a mixed race between Portuguese and Brazilians. No single colony in America is thought to contain so great a number of people of European descent.

Toward the end of the fifteenth century and through most of the sixteenth, Spain and Portugal were the two great naval powers on the ocean; for although the commerce of Venice reached every part of Europe, its fleet had scarcely ever sailed beyond the Mediterranean. The Spaniards, by right of first discovery, claimed all of America as their own; and although they could not stop a naval power as great as Portugal from settling in Brazil, such was the dread of their name at that time that most of the other nations of Europe were afraid to settle anywhere else on that great continent. The French who tried to settle in Florida were all murdered by the Spaniards. But the decline of Spanish naval power, following the defeat or failure of what they called their invincible armada toward the end of the sixteenth century, took away their ability to obstruct the settlements of other European nations any longer. So in the course of the seventeenth century the English, French, Dutch, Danes, and Swedes, all the great nations with ports on the ocean, attempted some settlements in the new world.

The Swedes settled in New Jersey; and the number of Swedish families still to be found there clearly shows that this colony was very likely to prosper had it been protected by the mother country. But, neglected by Sweden, it was soon swallowed up by the Dutch colony of New York, which in turn fell under English rule in 1674.

The small islands of St Thomas and Santa Cruz are the only territories in the new world ever held by the Danes. These little settlements too were under the government of an exclusive company that held the sole right both of buying the colonies' surplus produce and of supplying them with the foreign goods they needed, and which therefore, in both its buying and its selling, had not only the power to oppress them but the strongest temptation to do so. The government of an exclusive company of merchants is perhaps the worst of all governments for any country whatever. It was not, however, able to halt the progress of these colonies entirely, though it made it slower and more sluggish. The late king of Denmark dissolved this company, and since then the prosperity of these colonies has been very great.

The Dutch settlements in the West Indies, like those in the East Indies, were originally placed under the government of an exclusive company. So the progress of some of them, though considerable compared with that of almost any country long settled and established, has been sluggish and slow compared with that of most new colonies. The colony of Surinam, though very considerable, is still inferior to most of the sugar colonies of the other European nations. The colony of Nova Belgia, now divided into the two provinces of New York and New Jersey, would probably have soon become considerable too, even if it had remained under Dutch rule. The abundance and cheapness of good land are such powerful causes of prosperity that even the very worst government can scarcely check their effect completely. The great distance from the mother country also let the colonists evade, more or less, by smuggling, the monopoly the company held over them. At present the company allows all Dutch ships to trade with Surinam on paying two and a half per cent of the value of their cargo for a licence, and reserves to itself exclusively only the direct trade from Africa to America, which consists almost entirely of the slave trade. This relaxation of the company's exclusive privileges is probably the main cause of the prosperity the colony now enjoys. Curaçao and Eustatia, the two principal islands belonging to the Dutch, are free ports, open to the ships of all nations; and this freedom, in the midst of better colonies whose ports are open only to the ships of one nation, has been the great cause of the prosperity of those two barren islands.

The French colony of Canada was, during most of the last century and part of the present one, under the government of an exclusive company. Under such an unfavourable administration its progress was necessarily very slow compared with that of other new colonies; but it became much more rapid once this company was dissolved, after the collapse of what is called the Mississippi scheme. When the English took possession of this country, they found in it nearly double the number of inhabitants that father Charlevoix had assigned to it twenty or thirty years before. That Jesuit had travelled over the whole country and had no inclination to make it out as less important than it really was.

The French colony of Saint Domingo was founded by pirates and freebooters who for a long time neither sought the protection nor acknowledged the authority of France; and when that band of outlaws became citizens enough to acknowledge this authority, it had for a long time to be exercised very gently. During this period the population and improvement of the colony grew very fast. Even the oppression of the exclusive company to which it was for some time subjected, along with all the other French colonies, though it no doubt held it back, could not stop its progress entirely. Its prosperity resumed its course as soon as it was freed from that oppression. It is now the most important of the sugar colonies of the West Indies, and its output is said to be greater than that of all the English sugar colonies put together. The other French sugar colonies are generally all very thriving.
But no colonies have advanced more rapidly than the English ones in North America.
Plenty of good land, and the freedom to manage their own affairs their own way, seem to be the two great causes of the prosperity of all new colonies.

In the abundance of good land the English colonies of North America, though no doubt very well supplied, are nonetheless inferior to those of the Spaniards and Portuguese, and not superior to some of those held by the French before the late war. But the political institutions of the English colonies have been more favourable to the improvement and cultivation of this land than those of the other three nations.

First, the monopolizing of uncultivated land, though by no means prevented entirely, has been more restrained in the English colonies than in any other. The colony law obliges every owner to improve and cultivate a certain proportion of his lands within a set time, and, if he fails, declares those neglected lands available for granting to anyone else; and though it has perhaps not been very strictly enforced, it has had some effect.

Secondly, in Pennsylvania there is no right of primogeniture, and land, like movable property, is divided equally among all the children of a family. In three of the provinces of New England the eldest has only a double share, as in the law of Moses. So in those provinces, even if too much land should sometimes be monopolized by one individual, it is likely within a generation or two to be sufficiently divided up again. In the other English colonies, it is true, the right of primogeniture applies, as in the law of England; but in all the English colonies the tenure of the land, all of it held by free socage, makes it easy to sell, and the grantee of a large tract of land generally finds it in his interest to sell off as much of it as he can as fast as he can, keeping only a small quit-rent. In the Spanish and Portuguese colonies what is called the right of majorazzo applies to the succession of all those great estates to which any title of honour is attached. Such estates pass entirely to one person, and are in effect entailed and unsellable. The French colonies, it is true, are subject to the custom of Paris, which in the inheritance of land is much more favourable to the younger children than the law of England. But in the French colonies, if any part of an estate held by the noble tenure of chivalry and homage is sold, it is for a limited time subject to a right of redemption, either by the heir of the superior or by the heir of the family; and all the largest estates in the country are held by such noble tenures, which necessarily hamper their sale. But in a new colony a great uncultivated estate is likely to be divided up much faster by sale than by inheritance. The abundance and cheapness of good land, as already noted, are the main causes of the rapid prosperity of new colonies. Monopolizing land in effect destroys this abundance and cheapness. Monopolizing uncultivated land is also the greatest obstacle to its improvement; yet the labour spent on improving and cultivating land yields the greatest and most valuable produce to society. The produce of labour in this case pays not only its own wages and the profit of the capital that employs it, but also the rent of the land on which it is employed. So the labour of the English colonies, being more employed in the improvement and cultivation of land, is likely to yield a greater and more valuable produce than that of any of the other three nations, whose labour, through the monopolizing of land, is more or less diverted to other employments.

Thirdly, the labour of the English colonists is not only likely to yield a greater and more valuable produce, but, because of the moderation of their taxes, a greater proportion of this produce belongs to themselves, which they can store up and use to set still more labour in motion. The English colonists have so far never contributed anything toward the defence of the mother country or the support of its civil government. On the contrary, they themselves have so far been defended almost entirely at the expense of the mother country; and the expense of fleets and armies is out of all proportion greater than the necessary expense of civil government. The expense of their own civil government has always been very moderate. It has generally been limited to what was needed to pay adequate salaries to the governor, the judges, and a few other police officials, and to maintain a few of the most useful public works. The cost of the civil establishment of Massachusetts Bay, before the present disturbances began, used to be only about £18,000 a year; that of New Hampshire and Rhode Island, £3,500 each; that of Connecticut, £4,000; that of New York and Pennsylvania, £4,500 each; that of New Jersey, £1,200; that of Virginia and South Carolina, £8,000 each. The civil establishments of Nova Scotia and Georgia are partly supported by an annual grant of parliament; but Nova Scotia pays, besides, about £7,000 a year toward the public expenses of the colony, and Georgia about £2,500 a year. In short, all the various civil establishments in North America, excluding those of Maryland and North Carolina, of which no exact account has been got, did not, before the present disturbances began, cost the inhabitants more than £64,700 a year, an ever-memorable example of how cheaply three million people can be not only governed but well governed. The most important part of the expense of government, that of defence and protection, has constantly fallen on the mother country. The ceremony, too, of civil government in the colonies, on the reception of a new governor, the opening of a new assembly, and so on, though decent enough, is not accompanied by any costly pomp or parade. Their church government is run on an equally frugal plan. Tithes are unknown among them, and their clergy, who are far from numerous, are maintained either by moderate stipends or by the voluntary contributions of the people. The power of Spain and Portugal, by contrast, draws some support from the taxes levied on their colonies. France, indeed, has never drawn any considerable revenue from its colonies, since the taxes it levies on them are generally spent among them. But the colonial government of all three of these nations is run on a much more lavish plan and is accompanied by a much more expensive ceremony. The sums spent on receiving a new viceroy of Peru, for example, have often been enormous. Such ceremonies are not only real taxes paid by the rich colonists on those particular occasions, but they introduce among them the habit of vanity and extravagance on all other occasions too. They are not only very burdensome occasional taxes, but they help establish perpetual taxes of the same kind, still more burdensome: the ruinous taxes of private luxury and extravagance. In the colonies of all three of these nations, too, church government is extremely oppressive. Tithes apply in all of them, and are collected with the utmost rigour in those of Spain and Portugal. All of them, besides, are burdened with a numerous race of mendicant friars, whose begging, being not only licensed but sanctified by religion, is a most grievous tax on the poor people, who are most carefully taught that it is a duty to give to them and a very great sin to refuse them charity. On top of all this, in all of them the clergy are the greatest monopolizers of land.

Fourthly, in disposing of their surplus produce, or of whatever is over and above their own consumption, the English colonies have been more favoured, and allowed a wider market, than those of any other European nation. Every European nation has tried, more or less, to monopolize the commerce of its colonies for itself, and on that account has banned the ships of foreign nations from trading with them, and banned the colonies from importing European goods from any foreign nation. But the way this monopoly has been exercised has differed greatly from one nation to another.

Some nations have handed over the whole commerce of their colonies to an exclusive company, from which the colonists were obliged to buy all the European goods they wanted, and to which they were obliged to sell all their surplus produce. So it was in the company's interest not only to sell the former as dear, and buy the latter as cheap, as possible, but to buy no more of the latter, even at this low price, than it could resell for a very high price in Europe. It was in the company's interest not only to drive down in every case the value of the colony's surplus produce, but in many cases to discourage and hold down the natural growth of its quantity. Of all the schemes that could be devised to stunt the natural growth of a new colony, that of an exclusive company is undoubtedly the most effective. This, however, has been the policy of Holland, though in the course of the present century its company has in many respects given up exercising its exclusive privilege. This too was the policy of Denmark until the reign of the late king. It has at times been the policy of France; and lately, since 1755, after it had been abandoned by all other nations because of its absurdity, it has become the policy of Portugal, at least with regard to two of the chief provinces of Brazil, Pernambuco and Maranhão.

Other nations, without setting up an exclusive company, have confined the whole commerce of their colonies to one particular port of the mother country, from which no ship was allowed to sail except either in a fleet at a particular season, or, if alone, under a particular licence that in most cases was very well paid for. This policy did open the colony trade to all the natives of the mother country, provided they traded from the proper port, at the proper season, and in the proper ships. But since all the various merchants who pooled their capital to fit out those licensed vessels would find it in their interest to act in concert, the trade carried on in this way was bound to run on very nearly the same principles as that of an exclusive company. The profit of those merchants would be almost equally exorbitant and oppressive. The colonies would be poorly supplied, and forced both to buy very dear and to sell very cheap. This, however, was always the policy of Spain until within these few years; and the price of all European goods, accordingly, is said to have been enormous in the Spanish West Indies. At Quito, Ulloa tells us, a pound of iron sold for about 4s 6d, and a pound of steel for about 6s 9d sterling. But it is chiefly in order to buy European goods that the colonies part with their own produce. So the more they pay for the one, the less they really get for the other; the dearness of the one is the same thing as the cheapness of the other. The policy of Portugal in this respect is the same as the old policy of Spain toward all its colonies, except Pernambuco and Maranhão; and toward these it has lately adopted one still worse.

Other nations leave the trade of their colonies free to all their subjects, who may carry it on from all the various ports of the mother country and who need no other licence than the ordinary clearances of the custom-house. In this case the number and scattered locations of the various traders make it impossible for them to enter into any general combination, and their competition is enough to keep them from making very exorbitant profits. Under such a liberal policy the colonies are able both to sell their own produce and to buy European goods at a reasonable price; and ever since the dissolution of the Plymouth company, when our colonies were still in their infancy, this has always been the policy of England. It has generally been that of France too, and has uniformly been so since the dissolution of what in England is commonly called their Mississippi company. So the profits of the trade that France and England carry on with their colonies, though no doubt somewhat higher than they would be if the competition were open to all other nations, are by no means exorbitant; and the price of European goods, accordingly, is not extravagantly high in most of the colonies of either of those nations.

In exporting their own surplus produce, too, it is only with regard to certain goods that the colonies of Great Britain are confined to the market of the mother country. These goods, having been listed in the act of navigation and in some later acts, have on that account been called enumerated commodities. The rest are called non-enumerated, and may be exported directly to other countries, provided it is in British or plantation ships of which the owners and three quarters of the crew are British subjects.
Among the non-enumerated commodities are some of the most important products of America and the West Indies: grain of all kinds, lumber, salt provisions, fish, sugar, and rum.

Grain is naturally the first and chief object of cultivation in all new colonies. By allowing them a very wide market for it, the law encourages them to extend this cultivation far beyond the consumption of a thinly populated country, and so to provide in advance an ample subsistence for a continually growing population.

In a country entirely covered with forest, where timber is consequently of little or no value, the cost of clearing the ground is the main obstacle to improvement. By allowing the colonies a very wide market for their lumber, the law tries to make improvement easier by raising the price of a commodity that would otherwise be of little value, and so enabling them to make some profit on what would otherwise be pure expense.

In a country neither half populated nor half cultivated, cattle naturally multiply beyond the consumption of the inhabitants, and on that account are often of little or no value. But it is necessary, as already shown, that the price of cattle should bear a certain proportion to that of corn before most of the lands of any country can be improved. By allowing American cattle, in all forms, dead and alive, a very wide market, the law tries to raise the value of a commodity whose high price is so essential to improvement. The good effects of this freedom, however, must be somewhat reduced by the 4th of George III, c. 15, which puts hides and skins among the enumerated commodities and so tends to lower the value of American cattle.

To increase the shipping and naval power of Great Britain by expanding the fisheries of our colonies is an object the legislature seems to have had almost constantly in view. Those fisheries, on this account, have had all the encouragement that freedom can give them, and have flourished accordingly. The New England fishery in particular was, before the late disturbances, perhaps one of the most important in the world. The whale fishery, which despite an extravagant bounty is carried on in Great Britain to so little purpose that in the opinion of many people, which I do not, however, pretend to vouch for, its whole produce does not much exceed the value of the bounties paid for it annually, is carried on in New England without any bounty and to a very great extent. Fish is one of the chief articles with which the North Americans trade to Spain, Portugal, and the Mediterranean.

Sugar was originally an enumerated commodity, which could be exported only to Great Britain; but in 1751, on a petition from the sugar-planters, its export was permitted to all parts of the world. The restrictions under which this freedom was granted, however, combined with the high price of sugar in Great Britain, have made it largely ineffective. Great Britain and her colonies still continue to be almost the sole market for all the sugar produced in the British plantations. Their consumption is rising so fast that, although the import of sugar has greatly increased over the last twenty years thanks to the growing improvement of Jamaica and the ceded islands, the export to foreign countries is said to be not much greater than before.
Rum is a very important article in the trade the Americans carry on to the coast of Africa, from which they bring back African slaves in return.

If the whole surplus produce of America, in grain of all kinds, in salt provisions, and in fish, had been put on the enumerated list, and so forced into the market of Great Britain, it would have interfered too much with the produce of our own people's industry. It was probably not so much out of regard for America's interest as out of jealousy of this interference that these important commodities have not only been kept off the list, but that the import into Great Britain of all grain except rice, and of all salt provisions, has, in the ordinary state of the law, been prohibited.

The non-enumerated commodities could originally be exported to all parts of the world. Lumber and rice, having once been put on the enumerated list, were, when they were afterward taken off it, confined, as far as the European market goes, to the countries lying south of Cape Finisterre. By the 6th of George III, c. 52, all non-enumerated commodities were placed under the same restriction. The parts of Europe lying south of Cape Finisterre are not manufacturing countries, and we are less worried about the colony ships bringing home from them any manufactures that could compete with our own.

The enumerated commodities are of two kinds. First, those that are either peculiar to America, or cannot be produced, or at least are not produced, in the mother country. Of this kind are molasses, coffee, coconuts, tobacco, pimento, ginger, whalefins, raw silk, cotton, wool, beaver and other peltry of America, indigo, fustic, and other dye-woods. Secondly, those that are not peculiar to America but are, and can be, produced in the mother country, though not in quantities sufficient to supply most of her demand, which is chiefly met from foreign countries. Of this kind are all naval stores, masts, yards, and bowsprits, tar, pitch, and turpentine, pig and bar iron, copper ore, hides and skins, and pot and pearl ashes. The largest possible import of commodities of the first kind could not discourage the growth, or interfere with the sale, of any part of the mother country's produce. By confining them to the home market, our merchants, it was expected, would not only be able to buy them cheaper in the plantations, and so sell them at a better profit at home, but to establish between the plantations and foreign countries a profitable carrying trade, of which Great Britain would necessarily be the centre or emporium, being the European country into which those commodities were first to be imported. The import of commodities of the second kind might also be managed, it was supposed, so as to interfere not with the sale of the same kinds produced at home, but with that of the kinds imported from foreign countries; because, by means of suitable duties, they could be made always somewhat dearer than the home-produced kind, and yet a good deal cheaper than the foreign kind. So by confining such commodities to the home market, the aim was to discourage the produce not of Great Britain but of certain foreign countries with which the balance of trade was believed to be unfavourable to Great Britain.

The ban on exporting masts, yards, and bowsprits, tar, pitch, and turpentine from the colonies to any country but Great Britain naturally tended to lower the price of timber in the colonies, and so to increase the cost of clearing their lands, the main obstacle to their improvement. But around the start of the present century, in 1703, the pitch and tar company of Sweden tried to raise the price of their goods to Great Britain by banning their export except in their own ships, at their own price, and in such quantities as they thought fit. To counter this notable piece of commercial policy, and to make herself as far as possible independent not only of Sweden but of all the other northern powers, Great Britain gave a bounty on the import of naval stores from America; and the effect of this bounty was to raise the price of timber in America much more than confinement to the home market could lower it; and since both regulations were enacted at the same time, their combined effect was to encourage rather than discourage the clearing of land in America.

Although pig and bar iron, too, have been put among the enumerated commodities, yet since, when imported from America, they are exempt from considerable duties to which they are subject when imported from any other country, the one part of the regulation does more to encourage the building of furnaces in America than the other does to discourage it. There is no manufacture that uses up so much wood as a furnace, or that can contribute so much to the clearing of a country overgrown with it.

The tendency of some of these regulations to raise the value of timber in America, and so to make the clearing of the land easier, was perhaps neither intended nor understood by the legislature. But though their beneficial effects in this respect have been accidental, they have not on that account been any less real.

The most perfect freedom of trade is allowed between the British colonies of America and the West Indies, in both the enumerated and the non-enumerated commodities. Those colonies have now become so populous and thriving that each of them finds in some of the others a great and extensive market for every part of its produce. Taken all together, they form a great internal market for one another's produce.

England's liberality toward the trade of her colonies, however, has been confined chiefly to the market for their produce, either in its raw state or in what may be called the very first stage of manufacture. The more advanced or refined manufactures, even of the colony produce, the merchants and manufacturers of Great Britain choose to keep to themselves, and have persuaded the legislature to prevent their establishment in the colonies, sometimes by high duties and sometimes by outright prohibitions.

While, for example, Muscovado sugars from the British plantations pay only 6s 4d the hundredweight on import, white sugars pay £1 1s 1d, and refined sugar, whether double or single, in loaves, pays £4 2s 5⁸⁄₂₀d. When these high duties were imposed, Great Britain was the sole, and still continues to be the principal, market to which the sugars of the British colonies could be exported. So they amounted to a prohibition, at first of claying or refining sugar for any foreign market, and at present of claying or refining it for the market that takes off perhaps more than nine-tenths of the whole produce. So the manufacture of claying or refining sugar, though it has flourished in all the French sugar colonies, has been little carried on in any of the English ones, except for the colonies' own market. While Grenada was in French hands, there was a sugar refinery, working by claying, on almost every plantation. Since it fell into English hands, almost all works of this kind have been given up; and at present (October 1773) there are, I am assured, no more than two or three left on the island. At present, however, by an indulgence of the custom-house, clayed or refined sugar, if reduced from loaves into powder, is commonly imported as Muscovado.

Great Britain encourages the making of pig and bar iron in America by exempting it from the duties that the same goods pay when they come from any other country. Yet at the same time she absolutely forbids the building of steel furnaces and slitting mills in any of her American plantations. She will not let her colonies work in those more refined manufactures, not even to supply themselves, and instead insists that they buy every product of this kind they need from her own merchants and manufacturers.

She also bans the shipping of American-made hats, wools, and woollen goods from one province to another by sea, and even forbids carrying them overland on horseback or in a cart. This rule makes it effectively impossible to set up any manufacture of such goods for sale at a distance. It confines the colonists, in this line of work, to the same coarse household production that an ordinary family normally makes for its own use or for a few neighbours in the same province.

To forbid a great people from making the most of every part of their own produce, or from using their capital and labour in whatever way they think best for themselves, is a plain violation of the most sacred rights of mankind. Unjust as these prohibitions are, however, they have not so far done the colonies much harm. Land is still so cheap there, and therefore labour so expensive, that the colonists can import almost all the more refined or advanced manufactures from the mother country more cheaply than they could make them at home. So even if they had not been forbidden to set up such manufactures, in their present stage of development their own self-interest would probably have stopped them from trying. At this stage these prohibitions, perhaps, do not actually cramp their industry or push it away from any work it would have taken up on its own. They are simply insolent badges of slavery, imposed for no good reason by the baseless jealousy of the merchants and manufacturers of the mother country. In a more advanced stage, they could become genuinely oppressive and unbearable.

Just as Great Britain confines some of the colonies' most important products to her own market, so, by way of compensation, she gives some of those products an advantage in that market. Sometimes she does this by charging higher duties on the same goods when they come from other countries, and sometimes by paying bounties on their import from the colonies. In the first way she gives an advantage in the home market to the sugar, tobacco, and iron of her own colonies. In the second way she favours their raw silk, their hemp and flax, their indigo, their naval stores, and their building timber. This second method of encouraging colonial produce, by paying bounties on its import, is, as far as I have been able to learn, unique to Great Britain; the first is not. Portugal, for instance, is not satisfied with merely charging higher duties on tobacco imported from any other country, but prohibits it altogether under the harshest penalties.
When it comes to importing goods from Europe, England has likewise treated her colonies more generously than any other nation.

Great Britain allows part of the duty paid on imported foreign goods to be refunded when those goods are re-exported to a foreign country, almost always half, usually more, and sometimes the whole amount. It was easy to predict that no independent foreign country would take these goods if they arrived loaded with the heavy duties that almost all foreign goods pay on import into Great Britain. So unless some of those duties were refunded on re-export, the carrying trade would simply have ended, and the carrying trade was a trade the mercantile system greatly favoured.

Our colonies, however, are by no means independent foreign countries. Since Great Britain had claimed the sole right of supplying them with all European goods, she could have forced them, as other countries have forced their colonies, to take such goods loaded with all the same duties that they paid in the mother country. On the contrary, until 1763 the same refunds were paid on the re-export of most foreign goods to our colonies as to any independent foreign country. In 1763 this concession was significantly cut back by the act 4 Geo. III c. 15, which laid down “that no part of the duty called the old subsidy should be drawn back for any goods of the growth, production, or manufacture of Europe or the East Indies, which should be exported from this kingdom to any British colony or plantation in America; wines, white calicoes, and muslins, excepted.” Before this law, many kinds of foreign goods could be bought more cheaply in the plantations than in the mother country, and some still can.

It should be noted that the merchants who carry on the colony trade have been the chief advisers on most of the regulations governing it. We should not be surprised, then, if in much of this legislation their own interest has counted for more than that of either the colonies or the mother country. Through their exclusive right to supply the colonies with all the European goods they needed, and to buy up all the surplus colonial produce that did not compete with the trades the merchants carried on at home, the interest of the colonies was sacrificed to the interest of these merchants. And by allowing the same refunds on re-exporting most European and East India goods to the colonies as on re-exporting them to any independent country, the interest of the mother country was sacrificed to these merchants too, even by the mercantile standard of what that interest is. It was in the merchants' interest to pay as little as possible for the foreign goods they sent to the colonies, and therefore to recover as much as possible of the duties they had advanced on importing them into Great Britain. This let them sell the same quantity of goods in the colonies at a greater profit, or a greater quantity at the same profit, so they gained either way. It was also in the colonies' interest to get all such goods as cheaply and abundantly as possible. But this was not always in the mother country's interest. She often lost twice over: in her revenue, by refunding a large part of the duties paid on importing such goods, and in her manufactures, by being undercut in the colony market, because foreign manufactures could be shipped there so cheaply thanks to those refunds. It is commonly said that the growth of Great Britain's linen manufacture was considerably held back by the refunds on re-exporting German linen to the American colonies.

But although Great Britain's policy toward the trade of her colonies has been driven by the same mercantile spirit as that of other nations, it has on the whole been less illiberal and oppressive than any of theirs.

In everything except foreign trade, the English colonists are completely free to manage their own affairs in their own way. Their liberty is in every respect equal to that of their fellow citizens at home, and it is secured in the same way, by an assembly of the people's representatives, who claim the sole right of imposing taxes to support the colony government. The authority of this assembly keeps the executive power in check, and no colonist, however lowly or however offensive, has anything to fear from the anger of the governor or any other civil or military officer in the province, as long as he obeys the law. The colony assemblies, though, like the House of Commons in England, are not always a very fair representation of the people, yet they come closer to that ideal. And because the executive power either lacks the means to corrupt them, or, thanks to the backing it gets from the mother country, has no need to, they are probably more guided in general by the wishes of their constituents. The councils, which in the colony legislatures correspond to the House of Lords in Great Britain, are not made up of a hereditary nobility. In some colonies, as in three of the New England governments, these councils are not appointed by the king but chosen by the people's representatives. None of the English colonies has any hereditary nobility. In all of them, as in every free country, the descendant of an old colony family is more respected than an upstart of equal merit and fortune; but he is only more respected. He has no privileges by which he can trouble his neighbours. Before the present disturbances began, the colony assemblies held not only the legislative power but a share of the executive power as well. In Connecticut and Rhode Island they elected the governor. In the other colonies they appointed the revenue officers who collected the taxes those assemblies imposed, and those officers answered directly to the assemblies. There is therefore more equality among the English colonists than among the people of the mother country. Their manners are more republican, and their governments, especially those of three of the New England provinces, have so far been more republican too.

By contrast, the absolute governments of Spain, Portugal, and France carry over into their colonies. And the discretionary powers that such governments usually hand to their lower officers are, because of the great distance, naturally used there with more than ordinary violence. Under any absolute government there is more liberty in the capital than anywhere else in the country. The sovereign himself can never have any interest or wish to pervert justice or to oppress the great body of the people. In the capital, his presence holds his lesser officers more or less in awe, whereas in the remoter provinces, from which the people's complaints are less likely to reach him, those officers can tyrannize far more safely. But the European colonies in America are more remote than the most distant provinces of the greatest empires ever known before. The government of the English colonies is perhaps the only one in the history of the world that could give complete security to the people of so distant a province. The administration of the French colonies, however, has always been run with much more mildness and moderation than that of the Spanish and Portuguese. This better conduct suits both the character of the French nation and the thing that shapes the character of every nation, the nature of its government, which, although arbitrary and violent compared with Great Britain's, is lawful and free compared with those of Spain and Portugal.

It is in the progress of the North American colonies, however, that the superiority of English policy mainly shows itself. The progress of France's sugar colonies has been at least equal to, and perhaps greater than, that of most of England's. And yet England's sugar colonies enjoy a free government much like the one in her North American colonies. But France's sugar colonies are not discouraged, as England's are, from refining their own sugar. And, more important still, the character of the French government naturally leads to better treatment of their enslaved Africans.

In all European colonies, sugar cane is grown by enslaved Africans. It is assumed that people born in the temperate climate of Europe could not endure the labour of digging the ground under the burning sun of the West Indies. And growing sugar cane, as it is managed at present, is all hand labour, though many think the drill plough could be introduced into it with great advantage. But just as the profit and success of cultivation carried on by cattle depend heavily on managing those cattle well, so the profit and success of cultivation carried on by slaves must equally depend on managing those slaves well. And in managing their slaves the French planters are, I think it is generally agreed, superior to the English. The law, in so far as it gives some weak protection to the slave against the violence of his master, is likely to be better enforced in a colony whose government is largely arbitrary than in one that is wholly free. In every country where the wretched law of slavery exists, the magistrate, when he protects a slave, interferes to some degree in the management of the master's private property. In a free country, where the master may be a member of the colony assembly or an elector of such a member, the magistrate dares not do this except with the utmost caution and care. The respect he owes the master makes it harder for him to protect the slave. But in a country where the government is largely arbitrary, where the magistrate is used to interfering even in how individuals manage their private property, and may send them a lettre de cachet if they do not manage it as he likes, it is much easier for him to give the slave some protection, and common humanity naturally inclines him to do so. The magistrate's protection makes the slave less contemptible in his master's eyes, which leads the master to regard him with more consideration and treat him more gently. Gentle treatment makes a slave not only more loyal but more intelligent, and therefore more useful on both counts. He comes closer to the condition of a free servant, and may have some degree of honesty and loyalty to his master's interest, qualities that often belong to free servants but can never belong to a slave who is treated as slaves usually are in countries where the master is wholly free and secure.

That a slave's condition is better under an arbitrary government than under a free one is, I believe, borne out by the history of every age and nation. In Roman history, the first time we read of a magistrate stepping in to protect a slave from his master's violence is under the emperors. When Vidius Pollio, in the presence of Augustus, ordered one of his slaves who had committed a slight fault to be cut to pieces and thrown into his fish pond to feed his fish, the emperor angrily commanded him to free at once not only that slave but all the others he owned. Under the republic, no magistrate could have had the authority to protect the slave, much less to punish the master.

It should be noted that the capital which has improved France's sugar colonies, and the great colony of St Domingo in particular, has been built up almost entirely out of the gradual improvement and cultivation of those colonies. It has come almost wholly from the produce of the soil and the industry of the colonists, or, what amounts to the same thing, from the price of that produce, gradually accumulated by good management and used to raise still more produce. But the capital that has improved and cultivated England's sugar colonies has, for a large part, been sent out from England, and has by no means come entirely from the soil and industry of the colonists. The prosperity of the English sugar colonies has been largely due to the great wealth of England, part of which has overflowed, so to speak, onto these colonies. But the prosperity of France's sugar colonies has been due entirely to the good conduct of the colonists, which must therefore have had some superiority over that of the English; and this superiority has shown nowhere so clearly as in the good treatment of their slaves.
Such, in outline, has been the policy of the various European nations toward their colonies.
Europe's policy, then, has very little to boast about, either in the original founding of the American colonies or, as far as their internal government goes, in their later prosperity.

Folly and injustice seem to have been the guiding principles behind the first project of founding these colonies: the folly of chasing after gold and silver mines, and the injustice of coveting a country whose harmless natives, far from ever having injured the people of Europe, had welcomed the first adventurers with every sign of kindness and hospitality.

The adventurers who founded some of the later settlements did, it is true, add to the fanciful project of finding gold and silver mines other motives that were more reasonable and more admirable; but even these motives reflect very little credit on the policy of Europe.

The English Puritans, held down at home, fled to America for freedom and founded the four governments of New England there. The English Catholics, treated with far greater injustice, founded Maryland; the Quakers founded Pennsylvania. The Portuguese Jews, persecuted by the Inquisition, stripped of their fortunes, and banished to Brazil, brought, by their example, some sort of order and industry to the transported felons and prostitutes who originally peopled that colony, and taught them how to grow sugar cane. In all these cases it was not the wisdom and policy of the European governments but their disorder and injustice that peopled and cultivated America.

In carrying out some of the most important of these settlements, the various governments of Europe deserved as little credit as they did in planning them. The conquest of Mexico was the project not of the council of Spain but of a governor of Cuba, and it was carried out through the daring of the bold adventurer it was entrusted to, in spite of everything that governor, who soon regretted having trusted such a man, could do to thwart it. The conquerors of Chile and Peru, and of nearly all the other Spanish settlements on the American continent, took with them no public support beyond a general permission to make settlements and conquests in the name of the king of Spain. Those ventures were all at the private risk and expense of the adventurers. The government of Spain contributed hardly anything to any of them. The government of England contributed just as little toward establishing some of its most important colonies in North America.

Once these settlements were established and had grown large enough to attract the mother country's notice, the first regulations she made about them were always aimed at securing for herself a monopoly of their commerce, at confining their market and enlarging her own at their expense, and so at damping and discouraging rather than quickening and advancing their prosperity. The various ways in which this monopoly has been exercised make up one of the most basic differences in the policies of the different European nations toward their colonies. The best of them all, England's, is only somewhat less illiberal and oppressive than any of the rest.

In what way, then, has the policy of Europe contributed either to the first founding or to the present greatness of the American colonies? In one way, and one way only, it has contributed a great deal. Magna virum mater! It bred and shaped the men who were capable of achieving such great deeds and of laying the foundation of so great an empire; and there is no other part of the world whose policy is capable of forming, or ever actually has formed, such men. The colonies owe to the policy of Europe the education and broad outlook of their active and enterprising founders; and some of the greatest and most important of them, as far as their internal government goes, owe to it hardly anything else.
PART III. Of the Advantages which Europe has derived From the Discovery of America, and from that of a Passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope.
Such are the advantages the American colonies have gained from the policy of Europe.
What advantages has Europe gained from the discovery and colonization of America?

These advantages can be divided, first, into the general advantages that Europe, taken as one great country, has gained from those great events; and, second, into the particular advantages that each colonizing country has gained from the colonies that especially belong to it, through the authority or dominion it exercises over them.

The general advantages that Europe, taken as one great country, has gained from the discovery and colonization of America consist, first, in an increase of its enjoyments and, second, in a growth of its industry.

The surplus produce of America imported into Europe supplies the people of this great continent with a variety of goods they could not otherwise have had, some for convenience and use, some for pleasure, and some for ornament, and so adds to their enjoyments.
