It will readily be granted that the discovery and colonization of America have helped to increase the industry, first, of all the countries that trade directly with it, such as Spain, Portugal, France, and England; and, second, of all those that, without trading directly with it, send goods of their own produce there through other countries, such as Austrian Flanders and some provinces of Germany, which, through the countries just named, send it a considerable quantity of linen and other goods. All such countries have plainly gained a wider market for their surplus produce, and so must have been encouraged to increase it.

But that these great events should also have encouraged the industry of countries such as Hungary and Poland, which may perhaps never have sent a single product of their own to America, is not, perhaps, quite so obvious. That they have done so, however, cannot be doubted. Some of America's produce is consumed in Hungary and Poland, where there is some demand for the sugar, chocolate, and tobacco of that new part of the world. But those goods must be paid for with something that is either the produce of Hungarian and Polish industry, or something that had been bought with part of that produce. These American goods are new values, new equivalents, brought into Hungary and Poland to be exchanged there for the surplus produce of those countries. By being carried there, they create a new and wider market for that surplus produce. They raise its value, and so help to increase it. Even if no part of that surplus is ever carried to America, it may be carried to other countries that buy it with part of their share of America's surplus produce, and it may find a market through the circulation of the trade that was originally set in motion by America's surplus produce.

These great events may even have increased the enjoyments and the industry of countries that not only never sent any goods to America but never received any from it. Even such countries may have received a greater abundance of other goods from countries whose surplus produce had been increased by the American trade. This greater abundance, as it must have increased their enjoyments, so it must also have increased their industry. A greater number of new equivalents, of one kind or another, must have been offered to them in exchange for the surplus produce of that industry. A wider market must have been created for that surplus produce, raising its value and so encouraging its increase. The mass of goods thrown each year into the great circle of European commerce, and distributed each year by its various turnings among all the different nations within it, must have been enlarged by the whole surplus produce of America. A larger share of this larger mass is therefore likely to have fallen to each of those nations, increasing their enjoyments and their industry.

The exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to lessen, or at least to hold below what it would otherwise rise to, both the enjoyments and the industry of all those nations in general, and of the American colonies in particular. It is a dead weight on the action of one of the great springs that sets a large part of the business of mankind in motion. By making colonial produce dearer in all other countries, it reduces how much of it is consumed, and so cramps the industry of the colonies, along with both the enjoyments and the industry of all other countries, which enjoy less when they pay more for what they enjoy, and produce less when they get less for what they produce. By making the produce of all other countries dearer in the colonies, it cramps in the same way the industry of all other colonies, and both the enjoyments and the industry of the colonies. It is a clog that, for the supposed benefit of a few particular countries, hampers the pleasures and burdens the industry of all other countries, and of the colonies more than of any other. It not only shuts out all other countries as far as possible from one particular market, but confines the colonies as far as possible to one particular market; and there is a great difference between being shut out of one market while all others are open, and being confined to one market while all others are closed. Yet the surplus produce of the colonies is the original source of all the increase in enjoyments and industry that Europe gains from the discovery and colonization of America, and the exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to make this source far less abundant than it would otherwise be.

The particular advantages that each colonizing country gains from the colonies especially belonging to it are of two different kinds: first, the common advantages that every empire gains from the provinces under its rule; and, second, the special advantages supposed to come from provinces of such an unusual nature as the European colonies of America.

The common advantages that every empire gains from the provinces under its rule consist, first, in the military force they supply for its defence, and, second, in the revenue they supply to support its civil government. The Roman colonies occasionally supplied both. The Greek colonies sometimes supplied a military force but seldom any revenue. They rarely admitted themselves subject to the rule of the mother city. They were generally her allies in war but very seldom her subjects in peace.

The European colonies of America have so far never supplied any military force for the defence of the mother country. Their own military force has never even been enough for their own defence; and in the various wars the mother countries have fought, defending their colonies has generally diverted a very considerable part of those countries' military force. In this respect, then, all the European colonies without exception have been a source of weakness rather than of strength to their respective mother countries.

Only the colonies of Spain and Portugal have contributed any revenue toward the defence of the mother country or the support of her civil government. The taxes levied on the colonies of other European nations, and on those of England in particular, have seldom equalled the cost laid out on them in peacetime, and have never been enough to cover the cost they caused in wartime. Such colonies, therefore, have been a source of expense, not of revenue, to their respective mother countries.

The advantages of such colonies to their mother countries consist entirely in those special advantages supposed to come from provinces of such an unusual nature as the European colonies of America; and the exclusive trade, it is admitted, is the sole source of all those special advantages.

Because of this exclusive trade, all that part of the surplus produce of the English colonies, for example, which consists of what are called the enumerated commodities, can be sent to no country but England. Other countries must then buy it from her. It must therefore be cheaper in England than it can be anywhere else, and must add more to the enjoyments of England than to those of any other country. It must also do more to encourage her industry. For all those parts of her own surplus produce that England exchanges for these enumerated commodities, she must get a better price than any other country can get for the same parts of theirs when they exchange them for the same goods. England's manufactures, for example, will buy a greater quantity of her own colonies' sugar and tobacco than the same manufactures of other countries can buy of that sugar and tobacco. So far, then, as the manufactures of England and those of other countries are both to be exchanged for the sugar and tobacco of the English colonies, this advantage in price gives English manufactures an encouragement beyond what the others can enjoy in these circumstances. The exclusive trade of the colonies, then, just as it lessens, or at least holds below what they would otherwise rise to, both the enjoyments and the industry of countries that do not have it, so it gives a clear advantage to the country that does have it over those other countries.

This advantage, however, will perhaps turn out to be what may be called a relative rather than an absolute advantage, and to give the country that enjoys it a superiority by depressing the industry and produce of other countries, rather than by raising its own above what they would naturally reach under free trade.

The tobacco of Maryland and Virginia, for example, thanks to England's monopoly of it, certainly comes more cheaply to England than it does to France, to whom England usually sells a large part of it. But if France and all other European countries had always been allowed free trade with Maryland and Virginia, the tobacco of those colonies might by now have come cheaper, not only to all those other countries but to England as well. Tobacco production, given a market so much wider than any it has had so far, might, and probably would, by now have grown so much as to bring the profits of a tobacco plantation down to their natural level with those of a corn plantation, which they are supposed to be still somewhat above. The price of tobacco might, and probably would, by now have fallen somewhat lower than it is at present. An equal quantity of the goods of either England or those other countries might have bought a greater quantity of tobacco in Maryland and Virginia than it can now, and so have sold there for a better price. So far, then, as that weed can, by its cheapness and abundance, increase the enjoyments or the industry of England or of any other country, it would probably, under free trade, have done both to a somewhat greater degree than it does now. England, it is true, would in that case have had no advantage over other countries. She might have bought her colonies' tobacco somewhat cheaper, and so sold some of her own goods somewhat dearer, than she actually does; but she could neither have bought the one cheaper nor sold the other dearer than any other country might have done. She might perhaps have gained an absolute advantage, but she would certainly have lost a relative one.

To gain this relative advantage in the colony trade, however, to carry out the spiteful and malignant project of shutting out other nations as far as possible from any share in it, England, there are very good reasons to believe, has not only sacrificed part of the absolute advantage that she, like every other nation, might have gained from that trade, but has also brought upon herself both an absolute and a relative disadvantage in almost every other branch of trade.

When, by the Act of Navigation, England claimed for herself the monopoly of the colony trade, the foreign capital that had previously been employed in it was necessarily withdrawn. The English capital, which had before carried on only a part of that trade, now had to carry on the whole of it. The capital that had before supplied the colonies with only part of the European goods they wanted was now the only capital employed to supply them with the whole. But it could not supply the whole, and the goods it did supply were necessarily sold very dear. The capital that had before bought only part of the colonies' surplus produce was now the only capital employed to buy the whole. But it could not buy the whole at anything near the old price, and so whatever it did buy it necessarily bought very cheap. In a use of capital where the merchant sold very dear and bought very cheap, the profit must have been very great, and well above the ordinary level of profit in other branches of trade. This superior profit in the colony trade could not fail to draw away from other branches of trade part of the capital that had been employed in them. But this shift of capital, as it gradually increased the competition of capitals in the colony trade, must also have gradually reduced that competition in all those other branches; as it gradually lowered the profits of the one, so it gradually raised those of the others, until the profits of all came to a new level, different from, and somewhat higher than, the one at which they had stood before.

This double effect, of drawing capital away from all other trades and of raising the rate of profit somewhat higher than it otherwise would have been in all trades, was produced by this monopoly not only when it was first set up but has gone on being produced by it ever since.
First, this monopoly has been continually drawing capital away from all other trades to be employed in the colony trade.

Although the wealth of Great Britain has grown a great deal since the Act of Navigation was passed, it has certainly not grown in the same proportion as that of the colonies. But every country's foreign trade naturally grows in proportion to its wealth, and its surplus produce in proportion to its whole produce. And since Great Britain had taken to herself almost the whole of what may be called the colonies' foreign trade, while her own capital had not grown in the same proportion as the extent of that trade, she could not carry it on without continually withdrawing from other branches of trade some of the capital that had been employed in them, as well as withholding from them a great deal more that would otherwise have gone to them. Accordingly, ever since the Act of Navigation, the colony trade has been continually growing, while many other branches of foreign trade, especially the trade with other parts of Europe, have been continually declining. Our manufactures for foreign sale, instead of being suited, as before the Act of Navigation, to the nearby market of Europe or to the more distant one of the Mediterranean countries, have for the most part been adapted to the still more distant market of the colonies, the market where we have the monopoly rather than the one where we have many competitors. The causes of decay in other branches of foreign trade, which Sir Matthew Decker and other writers have looked for in excessive and poorly arranged taxation, in the high price of labour, in the growth of luxury, and so on, may all be found in the overgrowth of the colony trade. The mercantile capital of Great Britain, though very great, is not infinite, and though much increased since the Act of Navigation, has not increased in the same proportion as the colony trade. So that trade could not possibly be carried on without withdrawing some of that capital from other branches, and therefore without some decay of those other branches.

It should be noted that England was a great trading country, with a very large mercantile capital that was likely to grow greater every day, not only before the Act of Navigation had set up the monopoly of the corn trade but before that trade was even very considerable. In the Dutch war, under Cromwell's government, her navy was superior to that of Holland; and in the war that broke out at the start of Charles II's reign, it was at least equal, perhaps superior, to the combined navies of France and Holland. Its superiority would scarcely look any greater in the present day, at least if the Dutch navy now bore the same proportion to Dutch commerce that it did then. But this great naval power could not, in either of those wars, have been owing to the Act of Navigation. During the first war, the plan of that act had only just been drawn up; and though it had been fully enacted by legal authority before the second war broke out, no part of it could have had time to produce any considerable effect, least of all the part that set up the exclusive trade to the colonies. Both the colonies and their trade were small then, compared with what they are now. The island of Jamaica was an unhealthy desert, little inhabited and still less cultivated. New York and New Jersey were in the hands of the Dutch, and half of St Christopher's in those of the French. The island of Antigua, the two Carolinas, Pennsylvania, Georgia, and Nova Scotia had not been settled. Virginia, Maryland, and New England were settled; and although they were very thriving colonies, there was perhaps not at that time, in Europe or America, a single person who foresaw, or even suspected, the rapid progress they have since made in wealth, population, and improvement. In short, the island of Barbados was the only British colony of any importance whose condition then bore any resemblance to what it is now. The trade of the colonies, of which England enjoyed only a part even for some time after the Act of Navigation (for that act was not very strictly enforced until several years after it was passed), could not at that time have been the cause of the great trade of England, nor of the great naval power that trade supported. The trade that supported that great naval power at the time was the trade of Europe and of the Mediterranean countries. But the share of that trade that Great Britain now enjoys could not support any such great naval power. Had the growing trade of the colonies been left open to all nations, then whatever share of it might have fallen to Great Britain, and a very considerable share probably would have, must all have been an addition to the great trade she already had. Because of the monopoly, the increase of the colony trade has not so much added to the trade Great Britain had before as completely changed its direction.

Second, this monopoly has necessarily helped to keep the rate of profit in all the different branches of British trade higher than it naturally would have been if all nations had been allowed free trade with the British colonies.

The monopoly of the colony trade, as it necessarily drew toward that trade a greater proportion of Great Britain's capital than would have gone there of its own accord, so, by expelling all foreign capital, it necessarily reduced the whole amount of capital employed in that trade below what it would naturally have been under free trade. But by lessening the competition of capitals in that branch, it necessarily raised the rate of profit there. And by lessening the competition of British capitals in all other branches too, it necessarily raised the British rate of profit in all those other branches. Whatever the state or extent of Great Britain's mercantile capital may have been at any given moment since the Act of Navigation, the monopoly of the colony trade must, throughout that state, have raised the ordinary rate of British profit higher than it otherwise would have been, both in that trade and in all the other branches of British trade. If, since the Act of Navigation, the ordinary rate of British profit has fallen considerably, as it certainly has, it would have fallen still lower had the monopoly that act set up not helped to keep it up.

But whatever raises the ordinary rate of profit in any country higher than it otherwise would be necessarily places that country at both an absolute and a relative disadvantage in every branch of trade where it does not have the monopoly.

It places her at an absolute disadvantage, because in such branches of trade her merchants cannot get this greater profit without selling dearer than they otherwise would, both the foreign goods they import into their own country and the goods of their own country that they export abroad. Her country must both buy dearer and sell dearer; must both buy less and sell less; must both enjoy less and produce less than she otherwise would.

It places her at a relative disadvantage, because in such branches of trade it sets other countries, which are not under the same absolute disadvantage, either further above her or less below her than they otherwise would be. It lets them both enjoy more and produce more, in proportion to what she enjoys and produces. It makes their superiority greater, or their inferiority less, than it otherwise would be. By raising the price of her produce above what it otherwise would be, it lets the merchants of other countries undersell her in foreign markets, and so push her out of almost every branch of trade where she does not have the monopoly.

Our merchants frequently complain about the high wages of British labour as the reason their manufactures are undersold in foreign markets, but they say nothing about the high profits of capital. They complain of other people's excessive gains but say nothing of their own. Yet the high profits of British capital may, in many cases, do as much to raise the price of British manufactures as the high wages of British labour, and in some cases perhaps more.

It is in this way that the capital of Great Britain, one may fairly say, has been partly drawn and partly driven away from most of the branches of trade where she does not have the monopoly, and from the trade of Europe in particular, and of the Mediterranean countries.

It has partly been drawn away from those branches by the lure of higher profit in the colony trade, owing to the continual growth of that trade and the continual inability of the capital that carried it on one year to carry it on the next.

It has partly been driven away from them by the advantage that the high rate of profit prevailing in Great Britain gives to other countries, in all the branches of trade where Great Britain does not have the monopoly.

Just as the monopoly of the colony trade has drawn away from those other branches part of the British capital that would otherwise have been employed in them, so it has forced into them many foreign capitals that would never have gone there had they not been expelled from the colony trade. In those other branches of trade it has reduced the competition of British capitals, and so raised the rate of British profit higher than it otherwise would have been. On the contrary, it has increased the competition of foreign capitals, and so driven the rate of foreign profit lower than it otherwise would have been. In both ways it must plainly have placed Great Britain at a relative disadvantage in all those other branches of trade.

It may perhaps be said, however, that the colony trade is more advantageous to Great Britain than any other, and that the monopoly, by forcing into that trade a greater proportion of Great Britain's capital than would otherwise have gone there, has turned that capital into an employment more advantageous to the country than any other it could have found.

The most advantageous use of any capital to the country it belongs to is the one that maintains there the greatest quantity of productive labour and most increases the annual produce of that country's land and labour. But the quantity of productive labour that any capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption can maintain is exactly in proportion, as was shown in the second book, to how often its returns come in. A capital of a thousand pounds, for example, employed in a foreign trade of consumption whose returns come in regularly once a year, can keep constantly employed, in the country it belongs to, a quantity of productive labour equal to what a thousand pounds can maintain there for a year. If the returns come in twice or three times a year, it can keep constantly employed a quantity of productive labour equal to what two or three thousand pounds can maintain there for a year. A foreign trade of consumption carried on with a nearby country is, for this reason, generally more advantageous than one carried on with a distant country; and, for the same reason, a direct foreign trade of consumption is, as was likewise shown in the second book, generally more advantageous than a roundabout one.

But the monopoly of the colony trade, so far as it has affected the use of Great Britain's capital, has in every case forced some of it out of a foreign trade of consumption carried on with a nearby country into one carried on with a more distant country, and in many cases out of a direct foreign trade of consumption into a roundabout one.

First, the monopoly of the colony trade has, in every case, forced some of Great Britain's capital out of a foreign trade of consumption carried on with a nearby country into one carried on with a more distant country.

It has, in every case, forced some of that capital out of the trade with Europe and the Mediterranean countries into the trade with the more distant regions of America and the West Indies, from which the returns are necessarily less frequent, not only because of the greater distance but because of the peculiar circumstances of those countries. New colonies, as already noted, are always short of capital. Their own capital is always far less than what they could employ with great profit and advantage in improving and cultivating their land. They therefore have a constant demand for more capital than they have of their own, and to make up the shortfall they try to borrow as much as they can from the mother country, to whom they are consequently always in debt. The most common way the colonies run up this debt is not by borrowing on bond from the rich people of the mother country, though they sometimes do this too, but by running as much into arrears with their correspondents, who supply them with European goods, as those correspondents will allow. Their annual returns often do not amount to more than a third, and sometimes not even that proportion, of what they owe. The whole capital, therefore, that their correspondents advance to them is seldom returned to Britain in less than three years, and sometimes not in less than four or five. But a British capital of a thousand pounds, for example, that is returned to Great Britain only once in five years can keep constantly employed only a fifth of the British industry it could maintain if the whole were returned once a year; instead of the quantity of industry that a thousand pounds could maintain for a year, it can keep constantly employed only the quantity that two hundred pounds can maintain for a year. The planter, no doubt, by the high price he pays for European goods, by the interest on the bills he draws at distant dates, and by the commission on renewing those he draws at near dates, makes up, and probably more than makes up, all the loss his correspondent suffers from this delay. But although he makes up his correspondent's loss, he cannot make up that of Great Britain. In a trade whose returns are very distant, the merchant's profit may be as great or greater than in one whose returns are very frequent and near; but the advantage to the country he lives in, the quantity of productive labour constantly maintained there, the annual produce of its land and labour, must always be much less. That the returns of the trade to America, and still more of the trade to the West Indies, are generally not only more distant but more irregular and more uncertain than those of the trade to any part of Europe, or even of the Mediterranean countries, will, I imagine, be readily granted by anyone who has any experience of those different branches of trade.
Second, the monopoly of the colony trade has, in many cases, forced some of Great Britain's capital out of a direct foreign trade of consumption into a roundabout one.

Among the enumerated commodities that can be sent to no market but Great Britain, there are several whose quantity far exceeds the consumption of Great Britain, so that part of them must be exported to other countries. But this cannot be done without forcing some of Great Britain's capital into a roundabout foreign trade of consumption. Maryland and Virginia, for example, send to Great Britain each year more than ninety-six thousand hogsheads of tobacco, while the consumption of Great Britain is said not to exceed fourteen thousand. More than eighty-two thousand hogsheads, therefore, must be exported to other countries, to France, to Holland, and to the countries around the Baltic and Mediterranean seas. But that part of Great Britain's capital which brings those eighty-two thousand hogsheads to Great Britain, re-exports them from there to those other countries, and brings back from those other countries either goods or money in return, is employed in a roundabout foreign trade of consumption; and it is necessarily forced into this employment in order to dispose of this great surplus. If we wanted to work out in how many years the whole of this capital is likely to come back to Great Britain, we would have to add to the distance of the American returns the distance of the returns from those other countries. If, in the direct foreign trade of consumption we carry on with America, the whole capital employed often does not come back in less than three or four years, the whole capital employed in this roundabout one is not likely to come back in less than four or five. If the one can keep constantly employed only a third or a fourth of the domestic industry that could be maintained by a capital returned once a year, the other can keep constantly employed only a fourth or a fifth of that industry. At some of the outports, credit is commonly given to the foreign correspondents to whom the tobacco is exported. At the port of London, however, it is commonly sold for ready money: the rule is Weigh and pay. At the port of London, then, the final returns of the whole roundabout trade are more distant than the returns from America only by the time the goods may lie unsold in the warehouse, where, however, they may sometimes lie long enough. But had the colonies not been confined to the market of Great Britain for the sale of their tobacco, very little more of it would probably have come to us than was needed for home consumption. The goods that Great Britain now buys for her own consumption with the great surplus of tobacco she exports to other countries she would, in that case, probably have bought with the immediate produce of her own industry, or with some of her own manufactures. That produce, those manufactures, instead of being almost entirely suited to one great market, as at present, would probably have been fitted to a large number of smaller markets. Instead of one great roundabout foreign trade of consumption, Great Britain would probably have carried on a large number of small direct ones. Because of the frequency of the returns, a part, and probably only a small part, perhaps not more than a third or a fourth, of the capital that now carries on this great roundabout trade might have been enough to carry on all those small direct ones; might have kept constantly employed an equal quantity of British industry; and might have equally supported the annual produce of the land and labour of Great Britain. With all the purposes of this trade thus served by a much smaller capital, there would have been a large spare capital to apply to other purposes: to improve the land, to increase the manufactures, and to extend the commerce of Great Britain; to come into competition at least with the other British capitals employed in all those different ways, to lower the rate of profit in them all, and so to give Great Britain, in all of them, a superiority over other countries still greater than she now enjoys.

The monopoly of the colony trade, too, has forced some of Great Britain's capital out of all foreign trade of consumption into a carrying trade; and so, instead of more or less supporting the industry of Great Britain, that capital is now employed entirely in supporting partly that of the colonies and partly that of some other countries.

The goods, for example, that are bought each year with the great surplus of eighty-two thousand hogsheads of tobacco re-exported each year from Great Britain are not all consumed in Great Britain. Part of them, linen from Germany and Holland for example, is sent back to the colonies for their own consumption. But that part of Great Britain's capital which buys the tobacco with which this linen is afterwards bought is necessarily withdrawn from supporting the industry of Great Britain, to be employed entirely in supporting partly that of the colonies and partly that of the particular countries who pay for this tobacco with the produce of their own industry.

Beyond all this, the monopoly of the colony trade has pulled a far larger share of British capital toward that trade than would naturally have gone there, and in doing so it seems to have wrecked the natural balance that would otherwise have held among all the different branches of British industry. Instead of being fitted to a great many small markets, British industry has been shaped mainly to fit one great market. Instead of flowing through many small channels, British commerce has been trained to flow mainly through one great channel. The whole system of industry and commerce has thereby been made less secure, and the whole condition of the nation's body politic less healthy than it would otherwise be. As things now stand, Great Britain resembles one of those diseased bodies in which some vital organs have grown too large, and which for that reason are prone to many dangerous disorders that rarely strike a body whose parts are better proportioned. There is a great blood vessel here that has been swelled artificially beyond its natural size, and through it an unnatural share of the country's industry and commerce has been forced to circulate; a small blockage in it is very likely to bring on the most dangerous disorders throughout the whole body politic. That is why the prospect of a breach with the colonies has frightened the British people more than any Spanish armada or French invasion ever did. It was this fear, whether reasonable or not, that made the repeal of the Stamp Act a popular measure, at least among the merchants. Most of our merchants used to imagine that even a few years of total exclusion from the colony market would mean a complete halt to their trade; most of our master manufacturers imagined it would mean the utter ruin of their businesses; and most of our workmen imagined it would mean the end of their employment. A breach with one of our neighbours on the Continent, though it too would probably cause some halt or interruption in the work of all these groups, is contemplated without any such general panic. When circulation is blocked in some of the smaller vessels, the blood easily empties into the larger ones without causing any dangerous disorder; but when it is blocked in one of the larger vessels, convulsions, apoplexy, or death follow at once and cannot be avoided. If just one of those overgrown manufactures, raised by bounties or by the monopoly of the home and colony markets to some unnatural height, meets even a small halt or interruption in its work, it often sets off a riot and disorder that alarms the government and even disrupts the deliberations of the legislature. How great, then, people thought, must be the disorder and confusion that a sudden and total halt would necessarily cause in the work of so large a share of our principal manufacturers?

Some moderate, gradual loosening of the laws that give Great Britain her exclusive trade with the colonies, until that trade is largely free, seems to be the only way that can ever deliver her from this danger. It is the only thing that can enable her, or even force her, to pull some of her capital out of this overgrown employment and turn it toward other employments, even at lower profit. By gradually shrinking one branch of her industry and gradually expanding all the rest, it can by degrees restore every branch to that natural, healthy, and proper proportion which perfect liberty necessarily establishes and which perfect liberty alone can preserve. Throwing the colony trade open to every nation all at once might cause not only some passing inconvenience but a great and lasting loss to most of the people whose industry or capital is now tied up in it. Even the sudden loss of work for just the ships that import the eighty-two thousand hogsheads of tobacco that exceed Great Britain's own consumption could be felt very keenly. These are the unhappy effects of all the regulations of the mercantile system. They introduce very dangerous disorders into the body politic, and disorders that are often hard to cure without causing, for a time at least, still greater disorders. So I must leave it to the wisdom of future statesmen and legislators to decide exactly how the colony trade ought to be opened by degrees, which restraints ought to be lifted first and which last, and how the natural system of perfect liberty and justice ought to be restored step by step.

Five different events, none of them foreseen or expected, have very luckily come together to spare Great Britain from feeling, as keenly as everyone thought she would, the total exclusion that has now been in force for more than a year, since the first of December 1774, from a very important branch of the colony trade, that of the twelve associated provinces of North America. First, in getting ready for their non-importation agreement, those colonies stripped Great Britain completely of all the goods fit for their market. Second, the extraordinary demand of the Spanish flota has this year drained Germany and the north of many goods, linen in particular, which used to compete, even in the British market itself, with British manufactures. Third, the peace between Russia and Turkey has produced an unusual demand from the Turkey market, which had been very poorly supplied during the country's troubles and while a Russian fleet was cruising in the Archipelago. Fourth, the demand of northern Europe for British manufactures has been rising year by year for some time now. And fifth, the recent partition of Poland and the peace that followed it, by opening the market of that great country, have this year added an extraordinary demand from there to the growing demand of the north. All these events, except the fourth, are by their nature temporary and accidental, and the exclusion from so important a branch of the colony trade, if it unfortunately lasts much longer, may still cause some degree of distress. That distress, however, since it will come on gradually, will be felt far less sharply than if it had come all at once; and meanwhile the country's industry and capital may find a new employment and direction, so as to keep this distress from ever rising to any serious height.

So the monopoly of the colony trade, by turning a larger share of British capital toward that trade than would otherwise have gone there, has in every case turned it from a foreign trade of consumption with a nearby country into one with a more distant country; in many cases from a direct foreign trade of consumption into a roundabout one; and in some cases out of all foreign trade of consumption and into a carrying trade. In every case, then, it has shifted capital from a use in which it would have supported a greater amount of productive labour into one in which it can support far less. And by fitting so large a part of British industry and commerce to one particular market only, it has made the whole state of that industry and commerce more precarious and less secure than if their produce had been spread across a wider variety of markets.

We have to draw a careful distinction between the effects of the colony trade and the effects of the monopoly over that trade. The first are always and necessarily beneficial; the second always and necessarily harmful. But the first are so beneficial that the colony trade, even subject to a monopoly and despite all the harm that monopoly does, is still on the whole beneficial, and greatly so, though a good deal less than it would otherwise be.

In its natural and free state, the colony trade opens a great though distant market for those parts of British produce that exceed the demand of the markets nearer home, both in Europe and in the countries around the Mediterranean. In that natural and free state, the colony trade draws nothing away from those markets that they had ever received, and instead encourages Great Britain to keep increasing her surplus by continually offering new goods to exchange for it. In that natural and free state, the colony trade tends to increase the amount of productive labour in Great Britain without in any way changing the direction of the labour already employed there. In that natural and free state, the competition of all other nations would keep the rate of profit from rising above the common level, either in the new market or in the new employment. The new market would draw nothing from the old one; it would, so to speak, create a new produce to supply itself, and that new produce would form a new capital for carrying on the new employment, which likewise would draw nothing from the old one.

The monopoly of the colony trade does the opposite. By shutting out the competition of other nations, and thereby raising the rate of profit both in the new market and in the new employment, it pulls produce away from the old market and capital away from the old employment. The whole declared point of the monopoly is to enlarge our share of the colony trade beyond what it would otherwise be. If our share of that trade were going to be no larger with the monopoly than without it, there would be no reason to set up the monopoly at all. But anything that forces into a branch of trade, whose returns are slower and more distant than those of most other trades, a larger share of a country's capital than would go there of its own accord, necessarily makes the whole amount of productive labour kept up there each year, and the whole yearly produce of the country's land and labour, smaller than it would otherwise be. It holds the income of that country's inhabitants below the level it would naturally rise to, and thereby reduces their power to accumulate. It not only keeps their capital from supporting at all times as much productive labour as it would otherwise support, but keeps it from growing as fast as it would otherwise grow, and so from supporting a still greater amount of productive labour.

Yet for Great Britain the natural good effects of the colony trade more than make up for the bad effects of the monopoly, so that the trade, monopoly and all, even as it is carried on now, is not just advantageous but greatly so. The new market and the new employment that the colony trade opens are far larger than the slice of the old market and old employment lost to the monopoly. The new produce and new capital that the colony trade has, so to speak, created support in Great Britain a greater amount of productive labour than could have been thrown out of work by the pulling of capital away from other trades whose returns come more often. So if the colony trade is advantageous to Great Britain even as it is carried on now, it is not because of the monopoly but in spite of it.

It is the manufactured produce of Europe, rather than the raw, for which the colony trade opens a new market. Agriculture is the proper business of every new colony, a business that the cheapness of land makes more profitable than any other. New colonies therefore abound in the raw produce of the land, and instead of importing it from other countries they generally have a large surplus to export. In a new colony, agriculture either pulls hands away from every other occupation or keeps them from ever taking up another. Few hands can be spared for the necessary manufactures, and none for the ornamental ones. Most manufactures of both kinds the colonists find it cheaper to buy from other countries than to make for themselves. So it is mainly by encouraging the manufactures of Europe that the colony trade indirectly encourages its own agriculture. The European manufacturers employed by that trade form a new market for the produce of the land, and the most advantageous market of all, since the home market in Europe for corn and cattle, for bread and butcher's meat, is thus greatly enlarged through the trade to America.

But the examples of Spain and Portugal show clearly enough that the monopoly of the trade of populous, thriving colonies is not by itself enough to establish manufactures in a country, or even to keep them going. Spain and Portugal were manufacturing countries before they had any considerable colonies. Once they came to hold the richest and most fertile colonies in the world, both ceased to be manufacturing countries.

In Spain and Portugal the bad effects of the monopoly, made worse by other causes, have perhaps nearly outweighed the natural good effects of the colony trade. Those other causes seem to be monopolies of various other kinds; the lowering of the value of gold and silver below what it is in most other countries; the shutting out from foreign markets by misguided taxes on exports, and the narrowing of the home market by still more misguided taxes on moving goods from one part of the country to another; but above all the uneven and partial administration of justice, which often shields the rich and powerful debtor from the rightful claims of the creditor he has wronged, and which makes the industrious part of the nation afraid to prepare goods for those haughty grandees, whom they dare not refuse to sell to on credit and from whom they are wholly unsure of ever being paid.

In England, by contrast, the natural good effects of the colony trade, helped by other causes, have largely overcome the bad effects of the monopoly. Those causes seem to be: the general freedom of trade, which despite some restraints is at least equal, and perhaps superior, to that of any other country; the freedom to export almost every kind of domestically produced goods duty free to almost any foreign country; and, perhaps still more important, the unlimited freedom to carry them from one part of our own country to any other without having to report to any public office and without being liable to any kind of question or inspection; but above all the equal and impartial administration of justice, which makes the rights of the humblest British subject command respect from the greatest, and which, by securing to every man the fruits of his own labour, gives the strongest and most effective encouragement to every kind of industry.

So if British manufactures have advanced through the colony trade, as they certainly have, it has not been because of the monopoly but in spite of it. The effect of the monopoly has been not to increase the quantity of British manufactures but to alter the quality and shape of part of them, fitting to a market whose returns are slow and distant what would otherwise have been fitted to one whose returns are frequent and near. Its effect, therefore, has been to turn part of Britain's capital from a use in which it would have supported more manufacturing industry to one in which it supports much less, and thereby to reduce, instead of increase, the whole amount of manufacturing industry supported in Great Britain.

The monopoly of the colony trade, then, like all the other mean and malignant devices of the mercantile system, depresses the industry of every other country, and above all that of the colonies, without in the least increasing, but on the contrary diminishing, the industry of the country in whose favour it is set up.

The monopoly keeps that country's capital, whatever its size at any given moment, from supporting as much productive labour as it would otherwise support, and from yielding as great a revenue to the country's industrious inhabitants as it would otherwise yield. But since capital can grow only out of savings from revenue, the monopoly, by keeping it from yielding as great a revenue as it otherwise would, necessarily keeps it from growing as fast as it otherwise would, and consequently from supporting a still greater amount of productive labour and yielding a still greater revenue to the country's industrious inhabitants. So one great original source of revenue, the wages of labour, the monopoly must at all times have made less abundant than it would otherwise be.

By raising the rate of mercantile profit, the monopoly discourages the improvement of land. The profit from improvement depends on the difference between what the land actually yields and what, with a given amount of capital applied to it, it can be made to yield. If that difference offers a greater profit than an equal capital can earn in any mercantile employment, the improvement of land will draw capital away from all mercantile employments. If the profit is less, mercantile employments will draw capital away from land improvement. So anything that raises the rate of mercantile profit either narrows the advantage, or widens the disadvantage, of the profit from improvement; in the one case it keeps capital from going into improvement, in the other it draws capital out of it. By discouraging improvement, then, the monopoly necessarily retards the natural growth of another great original source of revenue, the rent of land. By raising the rate of profit, the monopoly also keeps the market rate of interest higher than it would otherwise be. But the price of land, relative to the rent it yields, the number of years' purchase commonly paid for it, necessarily falls as the rate of interest rises and rises as the rate of interest falls. So the monopoly hurts the landlord's interest in two ways: by retarding the natural growth, first, of his rent, and second, of the price he could get for his land in proportion to the rent it yields.

True, the monopoly raises the rate of mercantile profit and so somewhat increases the gains of our merchants. But because it obstructs the natural growth of capital, it tends to diminish rather than increase the total revenue that the country's inhabitants draw from the profits of stock, since a small profit on a great capital generally yields a greater revenue than a great profit on a small one. The monopoly raises the rate of profit, but it keeps the sum of profit from rising as high as it otherwise would.

All the original sources of revenue, the wages of labour, the rent of land, and the profits of stock, the monopoly makes much less abundant than they would otherwise be. To advance the small interest of one small order of men in one country, it injures the interest of every other order of men in that country and of all men in every other country.

It is only by raising the ordinary rate of profit that the monopoly has been, or could be, advantageous to any one particular order of men. But besides all the harm to the country in general that I have already shown must follow from a higher rate of profit, there is one further effect, perhaps more fatal than all the rest put together, and one that experience suggests is inseparable from it. A high rate of profit seems everywhere to destroy the thrift that in other circumstances comes naturally to the merchant's character. When profits are high, that sober virtue seems unnecessary, and lavish luxury seems better suited to the merchant's wealth. But the owners of the great mercantile capitals are necessarily the leaders and directors of a whole nation's industry, and their example influences the manners of the entire industrious part of the population far more than that of any other order of men. If his employer is careful and thrifty, the workman is very likely to be so too; but if the master is loose and disorderly, the servant, who shapes his work to the pattern his master sets, will shape his life too to the example his master gives. In this way accumulation is prevented in the hands of those who are naturally the most inclined to accumulate, and the funds meant to maintain productive labour get no addition from the revenue of those who ought to add the most to them. The country's capital, instead of growing, gradually dwindles, and the amount of productive labour it supports grows smaller every day. Have the exorbitant profits of the merchants of Cadiz and Lisbon increased the capital of Spain and Portugal? Have they eased the poverty, or promoted the industry, of those two impoverished countries? The tone of mercantile spending in those two trading cities has been such that those exorbitant profits, far from increasing the country's general capital, seem barely to have been enough even to keep up the capitals on which they were made. Foreign capitals are intruding more and more every day, so to speak, into the trade of Cadiz and Lisbon. It is to drive those foreign capitals out of a trade that their own grows daily less and less able to carry on that the Spaniards and Portuguese try every day to tighten the galling bands of their absurd monopoly. Compare the mercantile manners of Cadiz and Lisbon with those of Amsterdam, and you will see how differently the conduct and character of merchants are shaped by high profits and by low ones. The merchants of London, it is true, have not yet generally become such magnificent lords as those of Cadiz and Lisbon; but neither are they in general such careful, thrifty burghers as those of Amsterdam. Many of them are thought to be a good deal richer than most of the former, and not quite so rich as many of the latter; but the rate of their profit is commonly much lower than that of the former and a good deal higher than that of the latter. Light come, light go, says the proverb; and everywhere the ordinary level of spending seems to be set not so much by what one can really afford to spend as by how easily one supposes money can be got to spend.
So it is that the single advantage the monopoly gives to a single order of men proves, in many different ways, harmful to the general interest of the country.

To found a great empire for the sole purpose of raising up a people of customers may at first sight look like a project fit only for a nation of shopkeepers. It is, however, a project altogether unfit for a nation of shopkeepers, but perfectly fit for a nation whose government is run by shopkeepers. Only such statesmen are capable of imagining that they will gain something by spending the blood and treasure of their fellow citizens to found and maintain such an empire. Say to a shopkeeper, “Buy me a good estate, and I will always buy my clothes at your shop, even if I have to pay a bit more than I could elsewhere,” and you will not find him very eager to take you up on it. But if some other person buys you such an estate, the shopkeeper will be much obliged to your benefactor if he will require you to buy all your clothes at his shop. England bought, for some of her subjects who were unhappy at home, a great estate in a distant country. The price was in fact very small; instead of thirty years' purchase, the ordinary price of land nowadays, it came to little more than the cost of the various expeditions that made the first discovery, surveyed the coast, and took a token possession of the country. The land was good and vast in extent, and the settlers, with plenty of good ground to work and for a time free to sell their produce wherever they pleased, became, in little more than thirty or forty years, between 1620 and 1660, so numerous and thriving a people that the shopkeepers and other traders of England wanted to secure for themselves a monopoly of their custom. So, without even pretending that they had paid any part of either the original purchase money or the later cost of improvement, they petitioned Parliament that the cultivators of America should from then on be confined to their shop: first, to buy from them all the goods they wanted from Europe; and second, to sell to them all such parts of their own produce as those traders found it convenient to buy. For they did not find it convenient to buy every part of it. Some parts, imported into England, might have clashed with trades that they carried on themselves at home. Those particular parts, then, they were willing to let the colonists sell wherever they could, the farther off the better; and on that account they proposed that the colonists' market be confined to the countries south of Cape Finisterre. A clause in the famous Act of Navigation turned this thoroughly shopkeeper proposal into law.

Keeping up this monopoly has so far been the chief, or more truly perhaps the sole, end and purpose of the dominion that Great Britain claims over her colonies. The great advantage of provinces that have never yet supplied either revenue or military force for the support of the civil government or the defence of the mother country is supposed to lie in this exclusive trade. The monopoly is the main badge of their dependency, and it is the only fruit so far gathered from that dependency. Whatever Great Britain has so far spent in maintaining this dependency has really been spent in order to support this monopoly. Before the present disturbances began, the cost of the ordinary peacetime establishment of the colonies came to the pay of twenty regiments of foot; the cost of the artillery, stores, and extraordinary provisions needed to supply them; and the cost of a very considerable naval force kept up constantly to guard the immense coast of North America and that of our West Indian islands against the smuggling vessels of other nations. The whole cost of this peacetime establishment fell on the revenue of Great Britain, and was at the same time the smallest part of what dominion over the colonies has cost the mother country. To find the whole amount, we must add to the yearly cost of this peacetime establishment the interest on the sums that Great Britain has, on various occasions, laid out on the colonies' defence because she regarded them as provinces subject to her dominion. In particular we must add the whole cost of the late war and a great part of the cost of the war before it. The late war was entirely a colony quarrel, and its whole cost, in whatever part of the world it was spent, whether in Germany or the East Indies, ought in justice to be charged to the colonies' account. It came to more than ninety million pounds sterling, including not only the new debt that was contracted but the additional land tax of two shillings in the pound and the sums borrowed every year from the sinking fund. The Spanish war that began in 1739 was chiefly a colony quarrel too; its main object was to stop the searching of the colony ships that carried on a smuggling trade with the Spanish Main. This whole cost is really a bounty given to support a monopoly. Its pretended purpose was to encourage the manufactures and increase the commerce of Great Britain. But its real effect has been to raise the rate of mercantile profit and to enable our merchants to turn a larger share of their capital than they otherwise would into a branch of trade whose returns are slower and more distant than those of most other trades; two outcomes which, if a bounty could have prevented them, it might perhaps have been very well worth giving such a bounty.
So under the present system of management, Great Britain gets nothing but loss from the dominion she claims over her colonies.

To propose that Great Britain should voluntarily give up all authority over her colonies, and leave them to elect their own magistrates, make their own laws, and decide on peace and war as they thought fit, would be to propose a measure that no nation in the world ever has adopted or ever will. No nation ever voluntarily gave up dominion over any province, however troublesome it was to govern and however small the revenue it yielded compared with the cost it caused. Such sacrifices, though they might often serve a nation's interest, are always wounding to its pride; and, what is perhaps even more important, they always run against the private interest of the governing part of the nation, who would thereby lose the disposal of many places of trust and profit and many chances of gaining wealth and distinction, which possession of even the most turbulent and, to the mass of the people, the most unprofitable province seldom fails to provide. Even the most visionary enthusiasts could hardly propose such a measure with any serious hope of its ever being adopted. If it were adopted, however, Great Britain would not only be freed at once from the whole yearly cost of the colonies' peacetime establishment, but might settle with them such a treaty of commerce as would effectively secure her a free trade, more advantageous to the mass of the people, though less so to the merchants, than the monopoly she now enjoys. By thus parting as good friends, the natural affection of the colonies for the mother country, which our recent quarrels have perhaps all but extinguished, would quickly revive. It might dispose them not only to honour, for whole centuries, the treaty of commerce they had concluded with us at parting, but to favour us in war as well as in trade, and, instead of being turbulent and factious subjects, to become our most faithful, affectionate, and generous allies; and the same kind of parental affection on one side and filial respect on the other might revive between Great Britain and her colonies as once existed between the colonies of ancient Greece and the mother city from which they sprang.

For a province to be advantageous to the empire it belongs to, it ought in peacetime to yield the public a revenue sufficient not only to cover the whole cost of its own peacetime establishment but also to contribute its share to the support of the empire's general government. Every province necessarily adds, more or less, to the cost of that general government. So if a particular province does not contribute its share toward that cost, an unfair burden must be thrown on some other part of the empire. The extraordinary revenue that every province yields the public in wartime ought, by the same reasoning, to bear the same proportion to the empire's extraordinary revenue as its ordinary revenue does in peacetime. That neither the ordinary nor the extraordinary revenue Great Britain draws from her colonies bears this proportion to the whole revenue of the British empire will readily be granted. It has been supposed, indeed, that the monopoly, by increasing the private income of the British people and so enabling them to pay greater taxes, makes up for the shortfall in the public revenue of the colonies. But this monopoly, as I have tried to show, though a very heavy tax on the colonies, and though it may increase the income of a particular order of men in Great Britain, diminishes rather than increases that of the great body of the people, and consequently diminishes rather than increases the ability of the great body of the people to pay taxes. The men whose income the monopoly does increase, moreover, form a particular order which it is both absolutely impossible to tax beyond the proportion of other orders, and extremely impolitic even to try to tax beyond that proportion, as I shall try to show in the following book. So no special resource can be drawn from this particular order.
The colonies can be taxed either by their own assemblies or by the parliament of Great Britain.

That the colony assemblies could ever be so managed as to levy on their constituents a public revenue sufficient not only to maintain their own civil and military establishment at all times but also to pay their proper share of the cost of the British empire's general government seems very unlikely. It took a long time before even the parliament of England, set right under the sovereign's eye, could be brought under such a system of management, or made generous enough in its grants to support the civil and military establishments even of its own country. It was only by distributing among individual members of parliament a great part either of the offices, or of the disposal of the offices, arising from this civil and military establishment that such a system of management could be set up even with regard to the parliament of England. But the distance of the colony assemblies from the sovereign's eye, their number, their scattered situation, and their varied constitutions would make it very difficult to manage them in the same way, even if the sovereign had the same means of doing it; and those means are lacking. It would be utterly impossible to distribute among all the leading members of all the colony assemblies such a share, either of the offices or of the disposal of the offices, arising from the empire's general government, as to make them willing to give up their popularity at home and tax their constituents for the support of that general government, almost all the rewards of which would be shared out among people who were strangers to them. Besides, the administration's unavoidable ignorance about the relative importance of the different members of those different assemblies, the offences that must often be given, and the blunders that must constantly be made in trying to manage them this way, all seem to make such a system of management altogether impracticable with regard to them.

The colony assemblies, moreover, cannot be supposed to be the proper judges of what is needed for the defence and support of the whole empire. The care of that defence and support is not entrusted to them. It is not their business, and they have no regular way of being informed about it. A provincial assembly, like a parish vestry, may judge very properly about the affairs of its own particular district, but it has no proper means of judging about those of the whole empire. It cannot even judge properly about the proportion its own province bears to the whole empire, or about its relative wealth and importance compared with the other provinces, because those other provinces are not under the inspection and supervision of any particular province's assembly. What is needed for the defence and support of the whole empire, and in what proportion each part ought to contribute, can be judged only by the assembly that inspects and supervises the affairs of the whole empire.

It has accordingly been proposed that the colonies be taxed by requisition, with the parliament of Great Britain fixing the sum each colony ought to pay and the provincial assembly assessing and levying it in the way that best suited the circumstances of the province. In this way matters concerning the whole empire would be settled by the assembly that inspects and supervises the affairs of the whole empire, while each colony's provincial affairs might still be regulated by its own assembly. Even if the colonies in this case had no representatives in the British parliament, there is, judging by experience, no likelihood that the parliamentary requisition would be unreasonable. The parliament of England has never on any occasion shown the slightest inclination to overburden those parts of the empire that are not represented in it. The islands of Guernsey and Jersey, with no means of resisting the authority of parliament, are taxed more lightly than any part of Great Britain. In trying to exercise its supposed right, whether well or ill founded, of taxing the colonies, parliament has never yet demanded of them anything that even came close to a fair share of what was paid by their fellow subjects at home. Besides, if the colonies' contribution were to rise or fall in proportion to the rise or fall of the land tax, parliament could not tax them without taxing its own constituents at the same time, and the colonies might in that case be regarded as virtually represented in parliament.

There is no lack of examples of empires in which the different provinces are not all taxed, so to speak, in one lump, but in which the sovereign sets the sum each province ought to pay, and in some provinces assesses and levies it as he thinks fit, while in others he leaves it to be assessed and levied as the respective estates of each province determine. In some provinces of France the king not only imposes whatever taxes he pleases but assesses and levies them in the way he pleases. From others he demands a certain sum but leaves it to the estates of each province to assess and levy that sum as they think fit. Under the scheme of taxing by requisition, the parliament of Great Britain would stand toward the colony assemblies almost as the king of France stands toward the estates of those provinces that still enjoy the privilege of having estates of their own, the provinces of France that are supposed to be the best governed.

But though under this scheme the colonies would have no just reason to fear that their share of the public burdens would ever exceed the proper proportion to that of their fellow citizens at home, Great Britain might have just reason to fear that it would never reach that proper proportion. The parliament of Great Britain has not, for some time, had the same settled authority in the colonies that the French king has in those provinces of France that still enjoy the privilege of having estates of their own. The colony assemblies, if they were not very favourably disposed, and unless they were managed more skilfully than they ever have been so far, they are not very likely to be, might still find many pretexts for evading or rejecting even the most reasonable requisitions of parliament. Suppose a French war breaks out, and ten million pounds must be raised at once to defend the seat of the empire. This sum must be borrowed on the credit of some parliamentary fund pledged to pay the interest. Part of that fund parliament proposes to raise by a tax levied in Great Britain, and part of it by a requisition on all the different colony assemblies of America and the West Indies. Would people readily lend their money on the security of a fund that depended partly on the good humour of all those assemblies, far from the seat of the war and sometimes, perhaps, thinking themselves not much concerned in its outcome? On such a fund, probably no more money would be advanced than the tax to be levied in Great Britain could be supposed to cover. The whole burden of the debt contracted on account of the war would in this way fall, as it always has done so far, on Great Britain; on one part of the empire, and not on the whole empire. Great Britain is perhaps the only state since the world began that, as it has extended its empire, has only increased its expense without once increasing its resources. Other states have generally unloaded onto their subject and subordinate provinces the most considerable part of the cost of defending the empire. Great Britain has so far let her subject and subordinate provinces unload almost the whole of this cost onto her. To put Great Britain on a footing of equality with her own colonies, which the law has so far supposed to be subject and subordinate, it seems necessary, under the scheme of taxing them by parliamentary requisition, that parliament should have some means of making its requisitions immediately effective in case the colony assemblies should try to evade or reject them; and what those means might be is not very easy to imagine, and has not yet been explained.

And if the parliament of Great Britain were ever fully established in the right to tax the colonies, even without the consent of their own assemblies, the importance of those assemblies would from that moment be at an end, and with it the importance of all the leading men of British America. Men want a share in the management of public affairs chiefly for the importance it gives them. On the power that most of a country's leading men, its natural aristocracy, have of preserving or defending their respective importance depends the stability and lasting quality of every system of free government. The whole play of domestic faction and ambition consists in the attacks those leading men are continually making on one another's importance, and in the defence of their own. The leading men of America, like those of every other country, want to preserve their own importance. They feel, or imagine, that if their assemblies, which they like to call parliaments and to consider equal in authority to the parliament of Great Britain, were so far degraded as to become the humble ministers and executive officers of that parliament, most of their own importance would be gone. They have therefore rejected the proposal of being taxed by parliamentary requisition, and, like other ambitious and high-spirited men, have chosen rather to draw the sword in defence of their own importance.

Toward the decline of the Roman republic, the allies of Rome, who had borne the chief burden of defending the state and extending the empire, demanded to be admitted to all the privileges of Roman citizens. When this was refused, the Social War broke out. In the course of that war Rome granted those privileges to most of them, one by one, as they detached themselves from the general confederacy. The parliament of Great Britain insists on taxing the colonies, and they refuse to be taxed by a parliament in which they are not represented. Suppose that to each colony that detached itself from the general confederacy Great Britain were to grant such a number of representatives as matched its share of contribution to the empire's public revenue, on condition of its being subject to the same taxes and admitted, in compensation, to the same freedom of trade as its fellow subjects at home, the number of its representatives to grow as its share of contribution afterward grew; then a new way of gaining importance, a new and more dazzling object of ambition, would be set before the leading men of each colony. Instead of fiddling for the little prizes to be found in what might be called the paltry raffle of colony faction, they might then hope, with the confidence men naturally have in their own ability and good fortune, to draw some of the great prizes that sometimes come up on the wheel of the great state lottery of British politics. Unless this or some other method is hit upon, and there seems to be none more obvious than this, for preserving the importance and gratifying the ambition of the leading men of America, it is not very likely that they will ever willingly submit to us; and we ought to remember that the blood which must be shed in forcing them to submit is, every drop of it, the blood either of those who are, or of those whom we wish to have as, our fellow citizens. Those who flatter themselves that, in the state things have now reached, our colonies could be easily conquered by force alone are very weak. The men who now direct the resolutions of what they call their continental congress feel in themselves at this moment a degree of importance that perhaps the greatest subjects in Europe scarcely feel. From shopkeepers, tradesmen, and attorneys they have become statesmen and legislators, and are busy framing a new form of government for a vast empire, which they flatter themselves will become, and which indeed seems very likely to become, one of the greatest and most formidable that ever existed in the world. Five hundred different people, perhaps, who in various ways act directly under the continental congress, and five hundred thousand, perhaps, who act under those five hundred, all feel in the same way a proportional rise in their own importance. Almost every member of the governing party in America fills, at present, in his own imagination, a station higher not only than any he had filled before but than any he had ever expected to fill; and unless some new object of ambition is set before him or his leaders, if he has the ordinary spirit of a man, he will die defending that station.

President Hénault remarks that we now read with pleasure the accounts of many trifling transactions of the Ligue which, when they happened, were perhaps not thought of as very important news at all. But, he says, everyone then fancied himself of some importance; and the countless memoirs that have come down to us from those times were for the most part written by people who took pleasure in recording and magnifying events in which they flattered themselves they had been significant actors. It is well known how stubbornly the city of Paris defended itself on that occasion, and what a dreadful famine it endured rather than submit to the best, and later the most beloved, of all the French kings. Most of the citizens, or those who governed most of them, fought in defence of their own importance, which they foresaw would end the moment the old government was restored. Our colonies, unless they can be persuaded to agree to a union, are very likely to defend themselves against the best of all mother countries as stubbornly as the city of Paris defended itself against one of the best of kings.

The idea of representation was unknown in ancient times. When the people of one state were granted the right of citizenship in another, they had no way of exercising that right except by coming in a body to vote and deliberate with the people of that other state. The admission of most of the inhabitants of Italy to the privileges of Roman citizens completely ruined the Roman republic. It was no longer possible to tell who was and who was not a Roman citizen. No tribe could know its own members. A rabble of any sort could be brought into the assemblies of the people, could drive out the real citizens, and could decide the affairs of the republic as if they themselves had been citizens. But even if America were to send fifty or sixty new representatives to parliament, the doorkeeper of the House of Commons would have no great difficulty telling who was and who was not a member. So though the Roman constitution was necessarily ruined by the union of Rome with the allied states of Italy, there is not the least likelihood that the British constitution would be harmed by the union of Great Britain with her colonies. On the contrary, that constitution would be completed by it, and seems imperfect without it. The assembly that deliberates and decides about the affairs of every part of the empire ought certainly, in order to be properly informed, to have representatives from every part of it. I do not pretend that this union could be easily brought about, or that difficulties, and great difficulties, might not arise in carrying it out. I have not yet heard of any, however, that seem insurmountable. The chief ones, perhaps, arise not from the nature of things but from the prejudices and opinions of the people, on both sides of the Atlantic.

We on this side of the water are afraid that the multitude of American representatives might upset the balance of the constitution and increase too much either the influence of the crown on the one hand or the force of the democracy on the other. But if the number of American representatives were proportional to the produce of American taxation, the number of people to be managed would grow exactly in proportion to the means of managing them, and the means of managing in proportion to the number of people to be managed. The monarchical and democratic parts of the constitution would, after the union, stand in exactly the same relative strength toward one another as they had before.

The people on the other side of the water are afraid that their distance from the seat of government might leave them open to many oppressions; but their representatives in parliament, of whom the number ought to be considerable from the start, would easily be able to protect them from all oppression. The distance could not much weaken the dependence of the representative on his constituents, and he would still feel that he owed his seat in parliament, and all the importance he got from it, to their goodwill.
