It would therefore be in his interest to cultivate that goodwill by complaining, with all the authority of a member of the legislature, of every outrage that any civil or military officer might commit in those remote parts of the empire. Besides, the natives of America might flatter themselves, with some show of reason, that the distance from the seat of government would not last very long. Such has so far been that country's rapid progress in wealth, population, and improvement that in little more than a century, perhaps, the produce of American taxation might exceed that of British taxation. The seat of the empire would then naturally move to the part of the empire that contributed most to the general defence and support of the whole.

The discovery of America, and the discovery of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. Their consequences have already been great; but in the short span of two to three centuries that has passed since these discoveries were made, the full extent of their consequences cannot possibly have become clear. What benefits or what misfortunes to mankind may yet come from those great events, no human wisdom can foresee. By drawing the most distant parts of the world together to some degree, by enabling them to relieve one another's wants, increase one another's enjoyments, and encourage one another's industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial. To the natives, however, of both the East and West Indies, all the commercial benefits that may have come from those events have been swallowed up and lost in the dreadful misfortunes they caused. Those misfortunes, however, seem to have arisen from accident rather than from anything in the nature of the events themselves. At the particular time these discoveries were made, the superiority of force happened to be so great on the side of the Europeans that they were able to commit every kind of injustice in those remote countries with impunity. Hereafter, perhaps, the natives of those countries may grow stronger, or those of Europe may grow weaker; and the inhabitants of all the different quarters of the world may reach that equality of courage and force which, by inspiring mutual fear, can alone overawe the injustice of independent nations into some sort of respect for one another's rights. But nothing seems more likely to establish this equality of force than that mutual sharing of knowledge and of every kind of improvement which an extensive commerce among all countries naturally, or rather necessarily, carries with it.

Meanwhile, one of the chief effects of those discoveries has been to raise the mercantile system to a height of splendour and glory it could never otherwise have reached. The aim of that system is to enrich a great nation by trade and manufactures rather than by the improvement and cultivation of land, by the industry of the towns rather than that of the country. But as a result of those discoveries, the commercial towns of Europe, instead of being the manufacturers and carriers for only a very small part of the world, the part of Europe washed by the Atlantic and the countries around the Baltic and Mediterranean seas, have now become the manufacturers for the numerous and thriving cultivators of America, and the carriers, and in some respects the manufacturers too, for almost all the different nations of Asia, Africa, and America. Two new worlds have been opened to their industry, each of them much greater and more extensive than the old one, and the market of one of them growing greater and greater every day.

The countries that hold the colonies of America, and that trade directly to the East Indies, do enjoy all the show and splendour of this great commerce. Yet other countries, despite all the spiteful restraints meant to shut them out, often enjoy a greater share of its real benefit. The colonies of Spain and Portugal, for example, give more real encouragement to the industry of other countries than to that of Spain and Portugal. In the single item of linen alone, the consumption of those colonies comes, it is said (though I do not pretend to vouch for the quantity), to more than three million pounds sterling a year. But almost all of this great consumption is supplied by France, Flanders, Holland, and Germany. Spain and Portugal furnish only a small part of it. The capital that supplies the colonies with this great quantity of linen is annually distributed among, and yields a revenue to, the inhabitants of those other countries. Only the profits of it are spent in Spain and Portugal, where they help support the lavish extravagance of the merchants of Cadiz and Lisbon.

Even the regulations by which each nation tries to secure for itself the exclusive trade of its own colonies are often more harmful to the countries in whose favour they are made than to those against which they are made. The unjust oppression of the industry of other countries falls back, so to speak, on the heads of the oppressors and crushes their own industry more than it does that of the others. By these regulations, for instance, the merchant of Hamburg must send the linen he means for the American market to London, and bring back from London the tobacco he means for the German market, because he can neither send the one directly to America nor bring the other directly from there. This restraint probably forces him to sell the one somewhat cheaper and buy the other somewhat dearer than he otherwise might, and probably cuts his profits a little. Yet in this trade between Hamburg and London he certainly gets the returns on his capital much faster than he possibly could in the direct trade to America, even supposing, what is by no means the case, that American payments were as prompt as those of London. So in the trade to which these regulations confine the Hamburg merchant, his capital can keep employed a far greater amount of German industry than it possibly could in the trade from which he is shut out. Though the one employment may perhaps be less profitable to him than the other, it cannot be less advantageous to his country. It is quite otherwise with the employment into which the monopoly naturally draws, so to speak, the capital of the London merchant. That employment may perhaps be more profitable to him than most others; but because the returns are slow, it cannot be more advantageous to his country.

So after all the unjust attempts of every country in Europe to grab for itself the whole advantage of the trade of its own colonies, no country has yet managed to grab anything but the cost of supporting in peacetime, and defending in wartime, the oppressive authority it claims over them. The inconveniences that come from holding its colonies, every country has grabbed entirely for itself. The advantages that come from their trade, it has been forced to share with many other countries.

At first sight, no doubt, the monopoly of the great commerce of America naturally seems an acquisition of the highest value. To the undiscerning eye of giddy ambition it naturally appears, amid the confused scramble of politics and war, as a very dazzling thing to fight for. Yet the dazzling splendour of the object, the immense greatness of the commerce, is the very thing that makes the monopoly of it harmful, that makes one employment, in its own nature necessarily less advantageous to the country than most others, absorb a far greater share of the country's capital than would otherwise have gone to it.

The mercantile stock of every country, as was shown in the second book, naturally seeks, so to speak, the employment most advantageous to that country. If it is put into the carrying trade, the country it belongs to becomes the warehouse for the goods of all the countries whose trade that stock carries on. But the owner of that stock naturally wants to dispose of as much of those goods as he can at home. By doing so he saves himself the trouble, risk, and expense of exporting, and so he will be glad to sell them at home, not only at a much lower price but for a somewhat smaller profit, than he might expect by sending them abroad. He therefore tries as far as he can to turn his carrying trade into a foreign trade of consumption. And if his stock is put into a foreign trade of consumption, he will for the same reason be glad to dispose at home of as much as he can of the home goods he gathers up for export to some foreign market, and he will thus try as far as he can to turn his foreign trade of consumption into a home trade. In this way the mercantile stock of every country naturally courts the near employment and shuns the distant one; naturally courts the employment whose returns are frequent and shuns the one whose returns are distant and slow; naturally courts the employment in which it can support the greatest amount of productive labour in the country it belongs to, or where its owner lives, and shuns the one in which it can support the least there. It naturally courts the employment that in ordinary cases is most advantageous, and shuns the one that in ordinary cases is least advantageous to that country.

But if, in any one of those distant employments which in ordinary cases are less advantageous to the country, the profit should happen to rise somewhat higher than is enough to balance the natural preference given to nearer employments, this extra profit will draw stock away from those nearer employments until the profits of all return to their proper level. This extra profit, however, is proof that, in the society's actual circumstances, those distant employments are somewhat understocked compared with others, and that the society's stock is not distributed in the best way among all the different employments carried on in it. It is proof that something is either bought cheaper or sold dearer than it ought to be, and that some particular class of citizens is more or less oppressed, either by paying more or getting less than is consistent with the equality that ought to hold, and naturally does hold, among all the different classes of them. Though the same capital will never support as much productive labour in a distant employment as in a near one, a distant employment may be as necessary for the society's welfare as a near one, since the goods that the distant employment deals in may be necessary for carrying on many of the nearer employments. But if the profits of those who deal in such goods are above their proper level, those goods will be sold dearer than they ought to be, somewhat above their natural price, and everyone engaged in the nearer employments will be more or less oppressed by this high price. So their interest in this case requires that some stock be withdrawn from those nearer employments and turned toward the distant one, in order to bring its profits down to their proper level and the price of its goods down to their natural price. In this extraordinary case, the public interest requires that some stock be withdrawn from employments that in ordinary cases are more advantageous and turned toward one that in ordinary cases is less advantageous to the public; and in this extraordinary case the natural interests and inclinations of men coincide exactly with the public interest, just as they do in all other ordinary cases, and lead them to withdraw stock from the near employment and turn it toward the distant ones.

So it is that the private interests and passions of individuals naturally dispose them to turn their stock toward the employments that in ordinary cases are most advantageous to society. But if from this natural preference they should turn too much of it toward those employments, the fall of profit in them, and the rise of it in all others, immediately disposes them to correct this faulty distribution. So without any intervention of law, the private interests and passions of men naturally lead them to divide and distribute the stock of every society among all the different employments carried on in it as nearly as possible in the proportion most agreeable to the interest of the whole society.

All the different regulations of the mercantile system necessarily disturb, more or less, this natural and most advantageous distribution of stock. But those concerning the trade to America and the East Indies disturb it perhaps more than any other, because the trade to those two great continents absorbs more stock than any two other branches of trade. The regulations by which this disturbance is brought about in those two branches of trade, however, are not quite the same. Monopoly is the great engine of both, but it is a different sort of monopoly. Monopoly of one kind or another, indeed, seems to be the sole engine of the mercantile system.

In the trade to America, every nation tries to grab as much as it can of the whole market of its own colonies by openly shutting out all other nations from any direct trade with them. During most of the sixteenth century the Portuguese tried to manage the trade to the East Indies in the same way, claiming the sole right of sailing the Indian seas on the strength of having first found the way to them. The Dutch still keep all other European nations out of any direct trade with their spice islands. Monopolies of this kind are plainly set up against all other European nations, who are thereby not only shut out of a trade into which it might suit them to turn some of their stock, but are also forced to buy the goods that trade deals in somewhat dearer than if they could import them directly themselves from the countries that produce them.

But since the power of Portugal fell, no European nation has claimed the exclusive right of sailing the Indian seas, whose principal ports are now open to the ships of all European nations. Except in Portugal, however, and within these last few years in France, the trade to the East Indies has in every European country been put under an exclusive company. Monopolies of this kind are really set up against the very nation that creates them. Most of that nation are thereby not only shut out of a trade into which it might suit them to turn some of their stock, but are forced to buy the goods that trade deals in somewhat dearer than if it were open and free to all their countrymen. Since the founding of the English East India Company, for example, the other inhabitants of England, besides being shut out of the trade, must have paid, in the price of the East India goods they consumed, not only for all the extraordinary profits the company may have made on those goods through its monopoly, but for all the extraordinary waste that the fraud and abuse inseparable from managing the affairs of so great a company must necessarily have caused. So the absurdity of this second kind of monopoly is far more obvious than that of the first.
Both these kinds of monopoly disturb, more or less, the natural distribution of the society's stock; but they do not always disturb it in the same way.
Monopolies of the first kind always draw to the particular trade in which they are set up a larger share of the society's stock than would go to that trade of its own accord.

Monopolies of the second kind may sometimes draw stock toward the particular trade in which they are set up, and sometimes drive it away from that trade, depending on the circumstances. In poor countries they naturally draw to that trade more stock than would otherwise go to it. In rich countries they naturally drive away from it a good deal of stock that would otherwise go to it.

Such poor countries as Sweden and Denmark, for example, would probably never have sent a single ship to the East Indies if the trade had not been put under an exclusive company. Setting up such a company necessarily encourages adventurers. Their monopoly secures them against all competitors in the home market, and gives them the same chance in foreign markets as the traders of other nations have. Their monopoly shows them the certainty of a great profit on a considerable quantity of goods, and the chance of a considerable profit on a great quantity. Without such extraordinary encouragement, the poor traders of such poor countries would probably never have thought of risking their small capitals in so distant and uncertain an adventure as the trade to the East Indies must naturally have seemed to them.

Such a rich country as Holland, on the contrary, would probably, under free trade, send many more ships to the East Indies than it actually does. The limited stock of the Dutch East India Company probably drives away from that trade many great mercantile capitals that would otherwise go to it. The mercantile capital of Holland is so great that it is, as it were, continually overflowing, sometimes into the public funds of foreign countries, sometimes into loans to private traders and adventurers of foreign countries, sometimes into the most roundabout foreign trades of consumption, and sometimes into the carrying trade. All the near employments being completely filled, all the capital that can be placed in them at any tolerable profit being already placed there, the capital of Holland necessarily flows toward the most distant employments. The trade to the East Indies, if it were entirely free, would probably absorb the greater part of this surplus capital. The East Indies offer a market both for the manufactures of Europe and for the gold and silver, as well as for the various other products of America, greater and more extensive than Europe and America put together.

Every disturbance of the natural distribution of stock is necessarily harmful to the society in which it takes place, whether it drives away from a particular trade the stock that would otherwise go to it, or draws toward a particular trade stock that would not otherwise come to it. If, without any exclusive company, Holland's trade to the East Indies would be greater than it actually is, that country must suffer a considerable loss by having part of its capital shut out of the employment most convenient for that port. And in the same way, if, without an exclusive company, the trade of Sweden and Denmark to the East Indies would be less than it actually is, or, what is perhaps more likely, would not exist at all, those two countries must likewise suffer a considerable loss by having part of their capital drawn into an employment more or less unsuited to their present circumstances. It might be better for them, perhaps, as things now stand, to buy East India goods from other nations, even at a somewhat higher price, than to turn so large a part of their small capital to so very distant a trade, in which the returns are so very slow, in which that capital can support so little productive labour at home, where productive labour is so badly needed, where so little is done, and where so much is left to do.

So even if, without an exclusive company, a particular country could not carry on any direct trade to the East Indies, it would not follow that such a company ought to be set up there, but only that such a country ought not, in those circumstances, to trade directly to the East Indies. That such companies are not generally necessary for carrying on the East India trade is shown clearly enough by the experience of the Portuguese, who enjoyed almost the whole of it for more than a century together without any exclusive company.

It has been said that no private merchant could well have enough capital to keep factors and agents in the various ports of the East Indies to provide goods for the ships he might occasionally send there; and that unless he could do this, the difficulty of finding a cargo might often make his ships miss the season for returning, and the cost of so long a delay would not only eat up the whole profit of the venture but often cause a very considerable loss. But this argument, if it proved anything at all, would prove that no one great branch of trade could be carried on without an exclusive company, which is contrary to the experience of all nations. There is no great branch of trade in which the capital of any one private merchant is enough to carry on all the subordinate branches that must be carried on in order to carry on the principal one. But when a nation is ripe for any great branch of trade, some merchants naturally turn their capitals toward the principal branch and some toward the subordinate ones; and though all the different branches are in this way carried on, it very seldom happens that they are all carried on by the capital of one private merchant. So if a nation is ripe for the East India trade, a certain portion of its capital will naturally divide itself among all the different branches of that trade. Some of its merchants will find it in their interest to live in the East Indies and employ their capitals there in providing goods for the ships that are to be sent out by other merchants living in Europe. The settlements that different European nations have got in the East Indies, if they were taken from the exclusive companies they now belong to and put under the immediate protection of the sovereign, would make this residence both safe and easy, at least for the merchants of the particular nations to which those settlements belong. If at any particular time the part of a country's capital that of its own accord tended and inclined, so to speak, toward the East India trade was not enough to carry on all the different branches of it, that would be proof that, at that particular time, the country was not ripe for that trade, and that it would do better to buy for a while, even at a higher price, the East India goods it needed from other European nations, rather than import them itself directly from the East Indies. What it might lose by the high price of those goods could seldom equal the loss it would suffer by diverting a large part of its capital from other employments more necessary, more useful, or more suited to its circumstances and situation than a direct trade to the East Indies.

Though the Europeans hold many considerable settlements both on the coast of Africa and in the East Indies, they have not yet established in either of those countries colonies as numerous and thriving as those in the islands and on the continent of America. Africa, however, like several of the countries grouped under the general name of the East Indies, is inhabited by barbarous nations. But those nations were by no means as weak and defenceless as the wretched and helpless Americans; and, in proportion to the natural fertility of the countries they inhabited, they were besides much more populous. The most barbarous nations of either Africa or the East Indies were herdsmen; even the Hottentots were so. But the natives of every part of America except Mexico and Peru were only hunters; and there is a very great difference between the number of herdsmen and the number of hunters that the same extent of equally fertile land can support. In Africa and the East Indies, therefore, it was harder to displace the natives and spread the European plantations over the greater part of the lands of the original inhabitants. Besides, the character of exclusive companies is, as already noted, unfavourable to the growth of new colonies, and has probably been the chief cause of the little progress they have made in the East Indies. The Portuguese carried on the trade both to Africa and to the East Indies without any exclusive companies; and their settlements at Congo, Angola, and Benguela on the coast of Africa, and at Goa in the East Indies, though much depressed by superstition and every kind of bad government, still bear some resemblance to the colonies of America, and are partly inhabited by Portuguese established there for several generations. The Dutch settlements at the Cape of Good Hope and at Batavia are at present the most considerable colonies the Europeans have established in either Africa or the East Indies; and both those settlements are especially lucky in their situation. The Cape of Good Hope was inhabited by a race of people almost as barbarous, and quite as incapable of defending themselves, as the natives of America. It is, besides, the halfway house, so to speak, between Europe and the East Indies, at which almost every European ship stops for a while both going and returning. The supplying of those ships with every kind of fresh provisions, with fruit, and sometimes with wine, by itself provides a very extensive market for the surplus produce of the colony. What the Cape of Good Hope is between Europe and every part of the East Indies, Batavia is among the principal countries of the East Indies. It lies on the most frequented route from Hindostan to China and Japan, and is nearly midway along that route. Almost all the ships, too, that sail between Europe and China touch at Batavia; and beyond all this it is the centre and chief market of what is called the country trade of the East Indies, not only the part carried on by Europeans but the part carried on by the native Indians; and vessels manned by the inhabitants of China and Japan, of Tonquin, Malacca, Cochin-China, and the island of Celebes are frequently to be seen in its port. Such advantageous situations have enabled those two colonies to overcome all the obstacles that the oppressive character of an exclusive company may from time to time have put in the way of their growth. They have enabled Batavia to overcome the additional disadvantage of perhaps the most unhealthy climate in the world.

The English and Dutch companies, though they have established no considerable colonies except the two just mentioned, have both made considerable conquests in the East Indies. But in the way they both govern their new subjects, the natural character of an exclusive company has shown itself most plainly. In the spice islands the Dutch are said to burn all the spices a fertile season produces beyond what they expect to sell in Europe at the profit they think sufficient. In the islands where they have no settlements, they offer a reward to anyone who gathers the young blossoms and green leaves of the clove and nutmeg trees, which grow there naturally but which this savage policy has now, it is said, almost completely wiped out. Even in the islands where they have settlements, they have, it is said, greatly reduced the number of those trees. If the produce even of their own islands were much greater than suited their market, they suspect that the natives might find ways to convey some of it to other nations; and the best way, they think, to secure their own monopoly is to take care that no more shall grow than what they themselves carry to market. By various methods of oppression they have reduced the population of several of the Moluccas nearly to the number needed to supply fresh provisions and other necessaries of life to their own insignificant garrisons and to such of their ships as occasionally come there for a cargo of spices. Yet under the government even of the Portuguese, those islands are said to have been tolerably well inhabited. The English company has not yet had time to establish in Bengal so perfectly destructive a system. But the plan of their government has had exactly the same tendency. It has not been uncommon, I am well assured, for the chief, that is, the first clerk of a factory, to order a peasant to plough up a rich field of poppies and sow it with rice or some other grain. The pretext was to prevent a scarcity of provisions; but the real reason was to give the chief a chance to sell at a better price a large quantity of opium he happened then to have on hand. On other occasions the order has been reversed, and a rich field of rice or other grain has been ploughed up to make room for a plantation of poppies, when the chief foresaw that an extraordinary profit was likely to be made from opium. The servants of the company have on several occasions tried to set up in their own favour a monopoly of some of the most important branches, not only of the foreign but of the inland trade of the country. Had they been allowed to go on, it is impossible that they should not, at some time or other, have tried to restrict the production of the particular articles whose monopoly they had thus usurped, not only to the quantity they could buy themselves but to the quantity they could expect to sell at such a profit as they thought sufficient. In the course of a century or two, the policy of the English company would in this way probably have proved as completely destructive as that of the Dutch.

Yet nothing could be more directly contrary to the real interest of those companies, considered as the sovereigns of the countries they have conquered, than this destructive plan. In almost all countries the revenue of the sovereign is drawn from that of the people. So the greater the revenue of the people, the greater the annual produce of their land and labour, the more they can afford to give the sovereign. It is therefore in his interest to increase that annual produce as much as possible. But if this is the interest of every sovereign, it is especially the interest of one whose revenue, like that of the sovereign of Bengal, comes chiefly from a land rent. That rent must necessarily be in proportion to the quantity and value of the produce, and both of these must depend on the extent of the market. The quantity will always be suited, more or less exactly, to the consumption of those who can afford to pay for it, and the price they will pay will always be in proportion to the eagerness of their competition. So it is the interest of such a sovereign to open the widest possible market for the produce of his country, to allow the most perfect freedom of commerce, in order to increase as much as possible the number and competition of buyers; and on this account to abolish not only all monopolies but all restraints on carrying the home produce from one part of the country to another, on exporting it to foreign countries, or on importing goods of any kind for which it can be exchanged. In this way he is most likely to increase both the quantity and the value of that produce, and consequently his own share of it, that is, his own revenue.

But a company of merchants, it seems, is incapable of thinking of itself as sovereign, even after it has become one. They still regard trade, or buying in order to sell again, as their principal business, and by a strange absurdity treat the character of sovereign as a mere appendage to that of merchant, as something that ought to be made to serve it, or by means of which they may buy cheaper in India and so sell at a better profit in Europe. For this purpose they try as far as possible to keep all competitors out of the market of the countries under their government, and so to reduce at least some part of the surplus produce of those countries to what is barely enough to supply their own demand, or to what they can expect to sell in Europe at such a profit as they think reasonable. Their mercantile habits thus draw them, almost necessarily though perhaps unconsciously, to prefer on all ordinary occasions the small and passing profit of the monopolist to the great and lasting revenue of the sovereign; and would gradually lead them to treat the countries under their government nearly as the Dutch treat the Moluccas. It is the interest of the East India Company, considered as sovereigns, that the European goods carried to their Indian dominions be sold there as cheap as possible, and that the Indian goods brought from there fetch as good a price, or be sold there as dear, as possible. But the opposite of this is their interest as merchants. As sovereigns, their interest is exactly the same as that of the country they govern. As merchants, their interest is directly opposed to that interest.

But if the character of such a government is in this way essentially, and perhaps incurably, faulty even as regards its direction in Europe, that of its administration in India is still more so. That administration is necessarily made up of a council of merchants, a profession no doubt highly respectable, but which in no country in the world carries with it the sort of authority that naturally overawes the people and commands their willing obedience without force. Such a council can command obedience only by the military force that accompanies it, and its government is therefore necessarily military and despotic. Yet their proper business is that of merchants. It is to sell, on their masters' account, the European goods consigned to them, and to buy in return Indian goods for the European market; to sell the one as dear and buy the other as cheap as possible, and consequently to shut out, as far as possible, all rivals from the particular market where they keep their shop. So the character of the administration, as far as the company's trade is concerned, is the same as that of the direction. It tends to make government subservient to the interest of monopoly, and consequently to stunt the natural growth of at least some parts of the surplus produce of the country, down to what is barely enough to answer the company's demand.

All the members of the administration, besides, trade more or less on their own account, and it is useless to forbid them to do so. Nothing could be more completely foolish than to expect that a clerk in a great counting house, ten thousand miles away and therefore almost entirely out of sight, should, at a simple order from his masters, give up at once all business on his own account, abandon for ever all hopes of making a fortune for which he has the means in his hands, and content himself with the modest salaries his masters allow him, salaries which, modest as they are, can seldom be increased, since they are commonly as large as the real profits of the company's trade can afford. In such circumstances, to forbid the company's servants to trade on their own account can have scarcely any effect except to enable its superior servants, under pretext of carrying out their masters' orders, to oppress those inferior ones who have had the misfortune to fall out of favour. The servants naturally try to set up the same monopoly for their own private trade as for the public trade of the company. If they are allowed to act as they wish, they will set up this monopoly openly and directly, by simply forbidding all other people to trade in the articles they choose to deal in; and this is perhaps the best and least oppressive way of doing it. But if an order from Europe forbids them to do this, they will nonetheless try to set up a monopoly of the same kind secretly and indirectly, in a way that is far more destructive to the country. They will use the whole authority of government, and pervert the administration of justice, to harass and ruin anyone who interferes with them in any branch of commerce that, through agents either concealed or at least not openly acknowledged, they may choose to carry on. But the private trade of the servants will naturally extend to a far greater variety of articles than the public trade of the company. The public trade of the company reaches no further than the trade with Europe, and takes in only a part of the country's foreign trade. But the private trade of the servants may extend to all the different branches of both its inland and its foreign trade. The monopoly of the company can only stunt the natural growth of that part of the surplus produce which, under free trade, would be exported to Europe. That of the servants tends to stunt the natural growth of every part of the produce they choose to deal in, both what is meant for home consumption and what is meant for export, and so to degrade the cultivation of the whole country and reduce the number of its inhabitants. It tends to reduce the quantity of every kind of produce, even of the necessaries of life, whenever the servants of the country choose to deal in them, down to what those servants can both afford to buy and expect to sell at such a profit as pleases them.

From the very nature of their situation, too, the servants must be more disposed to uphold their own interest, against that of the country they govern, with rigorous severity than their masters can be to uphold theirs. The country belongs to their masters, who cannot help having some regard for the interest of what belongs to them; but it does not belong to the servants. The real interest of their masters, if they were capable of understanding it, is the same as that of the country; (the interest of every proprietor of India stock, however, is by no means the same as that of the country in whose government his vote gives him some influence. See book v, chapter 1, part ii.) and it is chiefly from ignorance, and from the meanness of mercantile prejudice, that they ever oppress it. But the real interest of the servants is by no means the same as that of the country, and the most perfect information would not necessarily put an end to their oppressions. Accordingly, the regulations sent out from Europe, though often weak, have on most occasions been well meaning. More intelligence, and perhaps less good meaning, has sometimes appeared in those made by the servants in India. It is a very singular government in which every member of the administration wants to get out of the country, and so to be done with the government, as soon as he can, and to whose interest, the day after he has left it and carried his whole fortune with him, it is perfectly indifferent though the whole country were swallowed up by an earthquake.

I do not mean, however, by anything I have said here, to cast any hateful slur on the general character of the servants of the East India Company, and still less on that of any particular persons. It is the system of government, the situation in which they are placed, that I mean to censure, not the character of those who have acted in it. They acted as their situation naturally directed, and those who have clamoured loudest against them would probably not have acted any better themselves. In war and negotiation, the councils of Madras and Calcutta have on several occasions conducted themselves with a resolution and decisive wisdom that would have done honour to the senate of Rome in the best days of that republic. Yet the members of those councils had been bred to professions very different from war and politics. But their situation alone, without education, experience, or even example, seems to have formed in them all at once the great qualities it called for, and to have inspired them with both abilities and virtues that they themselves could hardly know they possessed. So if on some occasions it has stirred them to acts of greatness that could hardly have been expected of them, we should not wonder if on others it has prompted them to deeds of a rather different nature.

Such exclusive companies, then, are nuisances in every respect: always more or less inconvenient to the countries in which they are established, and destructive to those that have the misfortune to fall under their government.
